bio.en: Eoghan McCabe is the co-founder and CEO of Intercom, the customer-service platform that he steered from a plateauing SaaS business into an AI-first company via its Fin AI agent, now on track to surpass $100 million in ARR.
bio.zh: Eoghan McCabe 是 Intercom 的联合创始人兼 CEO；他将这家客服平台从增长停滞的 SaaS 业务，通过 Fin AI 智能体转型为 AI 优先的公司，目前 Fin 的 ARR 正迈向 1 亿美元。

summary.en: Eoghan gets brutally honest about transforming Intercom into an AI-first company after growth nearly went negative, describing how he declared a 'wartime' mode and rewrote the company's values to cut out what wouldn't work in an AI era. He recounts pushing through intense resistance—including a soft coup attempt and roughly 40% staff turnover—to bet everything on Fin, an AI agent that hit eight figures in ARR within quarters. His core message: AI will disrupt your industry violently, so you must disrupt yourself first, and that requires a founder willing to make brave, hard decisions and own the results.
summary.zh: Eoghan 毫无保留地讲述了在增长几乎转负后，如何将 Intercom 转型为 AI 优先的公司：他宣布进入“战时”状态，并重写公司价值观，以剔除在 AI 时代不再有效的部分。他回顾了顶住巨大阻力（包括一次“软性政变”和约 40% 的人员更替）押注 Fin 的过程——这个 AI 智能体在几个季度内就达到八位数 ARR。他的核心观点是：AI 将以最猛烈的方式颠覆你的行业，所以你必须先自我革命，而这需要一个愿意做出勇敢、艰难决定并承担结果的创始人。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: You don't have a choice. AI is going to disrupt in the most aggressive violent ways. If you're not in it, you're about to get kicked out of all of it.
turns.zh: 你别无选择。人工智能将以最具侵略性、最暴力的方式颠覆行业。若你未能顺势而为，必将被彻底淘汰出局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have very successfully shifted late stage SaaS business to an AI-first agent-based business.

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Fin is our AI agent who will pass 100 million ARR with Fin in less than three quarters.
turns.zh: Fin是我们的AI智能代理，预计在不到三个季度的时间里，Fin业务将突破1亿美元年化经常性收入（ARR）大关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about how you made this actually happen.

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: We were about to hit $0 net new ARR, which means we would've been in negative growth territory.
turns.zh: 当时我们的净新增ARR即将跌至零，这意味着公司将陷入负增长的境地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, ChatGPT launches. Was it just like this is it, we got to go all in on this thing?

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I said, we need to become a wartime company. If we don't fight for this, we are dead. I jumped hard on AI, but I also restarted the culture. I rewrote the values designed to be a sharp knife to cut out the parts of the company that I just knew wouldn't be effective.
turns.zh: 我当时说道：我们必须成为一家战时状态的公司。如果不全力争取这块蛋糕，我们必将被淘汰。我大力推进AI战略的同时，还重塑了企业文化。重新制定了价值观体系，旨在用“快刀割肉”，彻底淘汰那些明显无法创造价值的部门。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you're trying to make the shift and it's just not moving, you may need to go hardcore founder mode.
turns.zh: 如果你试图转型却进展缓慢，或许需要开启创始人模式，全力以赴。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: The way that greatness is created is that you find a CEO who's willing to make brave hard decisions and own the results.
turns.zh: 伟大的企业之所以能诞生，是因为他们找到了愿意做出勇敢决策、并为结果负责的CEO。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have done something quite extraordinary with Intercom, something that a lot of founders and product teams are trying to do, which is to navigate this very scary disruption that's happening as a result of AI to most businesses. You have very successfully shifted, as you described, a late-stage SaaS business to an AI-first agent-based very successful business. I want to use the time to extract as much as I can out of your journey so that people that are trying to navigate this and having a hard time can have less pain, less suffering and will hopefully get to something that works. To give people a sense of just how well things have gone. Can you share some stats about the current state of the business, how it's going?
turns.zh: 你们在Intercom方面做得非常出色，这正是许多创始人和产品团队正努力应对的挑战——即如何应对AI给大多数企业带来的巨大变革冲击。正如你所描述的，你们成功地将一家处于后期阶段的SaaS企业转型为以AI为核心、基于智能客服的成功业务。我想利用这段时间尽可能深入解析你们的转型之路，让那些正艰难应对这一变革的人们能少走弯路，少受折磨，最终找到可行的解决方案。让我先带大家了解一下你们目前的业务成果，让大家对你们的成功有所直观认识。能否分享一下当前业务的数据，比如增长情况如何？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Currently across the business we benchmark ourselves against all public software companies. There's like 120 something B2B software companies. We're like in the 15th percentile for ARR growth, so we're up there. Fin, which is our AI agent, which is the future of the business, the thing that will disrupt the old business. It's growing north of 300%. It took off really fast like all these other AI companies you hear of the first year, it grew from one to 12 million ARR. We're now in solid mid eight digit ARR growth there, we'll pass 100 million ARR with Fin in less than three quarters. And yeah, Fin, we're in the customer experience category with Fin, so it's one of these agents that helps do all your customer work and they all started with service and in that category we are the biggest by customer count, biggest by revenue, best by performance benchmarks. We win all our head-to-heads and our direct competitor bake-offs. We're rated number one on G2, so I think we're doing pretty well. We're doing far better than we imagined at this point.
turns.zh: 目前，我们将自己与所有上市软件公司进行比较。大约有120多家B2B软件公司。我们在ARR增长方面处于前15%的水平，所以表现相当不错。Fin（我们的AI客服平台）是公司的未来，它将颠覆传统业务模式。目前其增长率超过300%。正如你所知，许多AI公司在第一年就能实现飞速增长，Fin从0到1200万ARR仅用了一年时间。如今，Fin的ARR增长率稳定在8位数水平，预计不到三个季度就能突破1亿ARR大关。Fin属于客户体验类别，是帮助处理客户工作的智能客服平台之一。在这一领域，我们以客户数量和收入规模领跑市场，各项性能基准表现优异。在与竞争对手的对决和方案比拼中我们始终胜出，还在G2平台上荣获第一名。我认为我们的表现远超预期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. This sounds like the dream for a lot of founders, especially ones that are stuck with their existing business that isn't going very far. So, let's get to that. Let's talk about the beginning of this journey. You had a business that was working, people used it, loved it, over 100 million ARR I believe. Talk about just the state of the business at the point roughly when you decided I really need to make a big change and go AI first.
turns.zh: 好的。这听起来像是许多创始人的梦想，尤其是那些被现有业务困住、难以突破的创业者。所以，接下来就来聊聊这段旅程的开端吧。你们原本有一项运转良好的业务，用户反馈良好，ARR超过1亿。据我所知，你们当时面临着一个关键决策——是彻底转型还是维持现状？能否谈谈在决定转向AI优先战略时，业务的具体状况？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: It was already in the hundreds of millions, Intercom is 14 years and change now. Part of the story is that in 2020 I had been sick for a couple years. The background is I had mold toxins and later I found out that I got a tick bite and that messed me up. And so I left the CEO role in 2020 and a lot of the mistakes I had been making when I was sick got worse. We became what a lot of late stage software companies are today, which is a bit bloated. We lost some energy. Our strategy was diluted and unfocused. We're trying to do all the things for all the people. (00:08:06): We didn't know what problems we were already solving and for who, and the result was very slow revenue growth in the low single digit percent and I was away for two years unsatisfied where the business was going. We had this post COVID sugar rush, which a lot of big companies at that stage did in 2021. Everyone's valuation and revenue was through the roof and that hit a lot of problems in a lot of these companies and we had five quarters of success of sequential decline in our net new ARR and we were about to hit $0 net new ARR which means we would've in negative growth territory. We never got there. I managed to stop it before we got there, but we were falling each quarter and I found that I, despite my wishes to go and have new adventures, still had a lot of pride for this damn thing and didn't want to see it. (00:09:15): And in a way that was so different from the way it started, it started with so much hope and optimism like so many companies do, and it was about to fade away. So, that was when I felt like I need to go back and I need to make a change. I went back and one month later ChatGPT was announced, so it would be really neat and tidy to be able to say that the AI transformation came, I knew I couldn't be on the sidelines, I had to save this thing from the coming disruption. Actually, I got whacked across the head by this AI thing, but it also ended up being a gift.
turns.zh: 当时我们的用户已经达到了数亿级别，而Intercom如今已有14年历史。故事的背景是，2020年我生病了好几年。起因是吸入了霉菌毒素，后来发现自己被蜱虫叮咬了，这让我的健康每况愈下。因此，我在2020年辞去了CEO职务，而我在生病期间犯下的许多错误也愈发严重。我们逐渐陷入了许多后期软件公司如今的困境——机构臃肿、精力分散、战略模糊、试图面面俱到。（00:08:06）：我们既不清楚自己在解决哪些问题，也不清楚服务的目标客户是谁。结果是收入增长极其缓慢，低个位数百分比的增速让我对业务走向感到失望。2021年COVID疫情后，一些大公司曾短暂迎来估值和收入暴涨，但这种泡沫最终导致许多公司遭遇困境。我们经历了连续五个季度净新ARR（年度经常性收入）下滑，差点跌至零点，意味着陷入负增长。所幸我及时止住了颓势，但每季度都在下滑。尽管我渴望开启新征程，但对这家公司的自豪感让我不愿眼睁睁看着它消亡。（00:09:15）：与最初的愿景相去甚远。当初我们和许多公司一样满怀希望，然而如今却面临崩盘的危机。于是我决定回归，重新规划。一个月后，ChatGPT横空出世。要是能说AI变革由此启程，那真是再完美不过了。我深知不能置身事外，要从即将来临的变革中拯救这家公司。说实话，我被AI浪潮彻底冲击，但最终它也成为一项天赐的机遇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, ChatGPT launches, was it just like this is it, we got to go all in on this thing? Was it like, hmm, let's watch this thing? How quickly was it clear that this is the future, this isn't working what we're doing?
turns.zh: 那么，ChatGPT问世后，大家是如何应对的？是那种“这就是未来了，必须全力押注”的决心？还是“先观望观望再说”的谨慎态度？又或者是如何迅速意识到现有策略已然落伍？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: We and I were very lucky and that we had an AI group already. We were in the customer communication business, chiefly doing customer service. We were building bots, but they were rudimentary AI. We had a bunch of our own machine learning that did Q&A for customer service, but it required a phenomenal amount of setup and was kind of crappy. But we had a number of AI engineers in the company already, and so when GPT 3.5 came out, they said, this is different and it didn't take long for people to start to imagine that this is going to be pretty disruptive to service. And it started where we imagined that this was going to just wreck everyone selling seats, everyone in the conventional SaaS game. (00:10:52): And we believed that was quite possible for some couple years after that moment. But we were only six weeks into the launch of GPT 3.5 when we actually had a beta version of Fin. I got a text from Des, my co-founder, a week or so after the launch of GPT 3.5 and he said, "The AI team have something interesting and they actually think we could make a product out of this." And this was long before there's now no doubt 100 service agents. We had something very early working and part of what we had to our advantage also was that we had this giant base 300, sorry, 30,000 paying customers, hundreds of thousands of active users, millions of their users, billions of data points. (00:11:42): So, we had a lot to play with and so we jumped on it. Now obviously it's fun to tell that once again to the idea of this brave Maverick move, and I won't discount the fact that we were brave, but we were coming from a point of having nothing to lose. So, we certainly are unique. I don't know a single company of our size and age that has pivoted this hard to AI and being as successful as we have been, but we also previously were screwed. We were in a really tough spot, so had no choice. So, I'll take the kudos and credit, but also have a lot of empathy for companies that weren't as in as much trouble as we were, and so try to thread the needle and sustain the old business while adding to it with the new AI stuff.
turns.zh:
当时我们和团队非常幸运，因为公司已经组建了一个AI团队。我们当时从事客户沟通业务，主要负责客服工作。我们开发过一些机器人，但那只是初级的人工智能。我们有一些自主研发的机器学习技术，用于客服问答，但这需要耗费大量精力调试，效果也相当糟糕。不过公司里已经有几位AI工程师，所以当GPT 3.5推出时，他们意识到这项技术将彻底颠覆客户服务行业。最初我们以为这只会冲击传统的SaaS服务商，比如座位销售商之类的。（00:10:52）在GPT 3.5发布后几周，我们就推出了Fin的测试版。GPT 3.5刚上线一周左右，我收到了联合创始人Des的短信，他说"AI团队有一些很有趣的成果，他们觉得我们能基于此开发出一款产品。"这时候我们还没有100名客服代理，远远不够。我们的早期版本已经能运行了，而且我们还有一个庞大的用户基础——3万付费客户、数十万活跃用户、数百万用户数据、数十亿数据点。

（00:11:42）显然，回顾这段经历，人们会惊叹于我们大胆的转变。我不否认我们确实有勇气，但当时我们其实没什么可失去的。所以我们抓住了机遇。当然，回想起来，这确实是个大胆的冒险，但我们当时确实别无选择。我们之前的处境非常艰难，必须要做出改变。我会欣然接受赞誉，但也对那些没有我们这么深陷困境的公司心怀同理。我们努力在维持原有业务的同时，通过AI技术实现升级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I heard from someone that worked at Intercom, correct me if this is not correct, you've always been very anti-bot in the customer support business because you didn't like how impersonal it was. It just didn't feel like the way you wanted to build a business, and then now that's what you do. Talk about just that transition.
turns.zh: 我从Intercom的一位前员工那里听说，他们在客服领域一直反对使用机器人，因为觉得那太没有人性化了。这根本不是他们想打造的业务模式，但现在他们却在做这件事。能谈谈这种转变吗？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah, I know it's a fun and ironic twist. Our mission from the early days was make internet business personal. And when I came back and we started to lean into AI, I started to wonder, does that mission make any sense anymore? Now, part of our lean into AI is that we had no choice not only for the business, we needed something new, but also we saw that this is the future and you can't fight the future. You must be part of it. And so okay, fuck, we're going to be part of it. And ultimately, and it's very easy to tell yourself these little stories. So, I'm open to anyone telling me this is bullshit, but when I interrogate myself, my soul and my mind, I don't think it is, when I interrogate my heart and my mind, I don't think it is. (00:13:43): But I'm now of the belief that providing a customer with a highly engaged, instantly available expert, consistent, fast, charismatic, funny, friendly, personal agent available for literally every single customer every minute of the day around the clock is so much more personal than making them wait 2, 3, 4 days for a crappy canned response. And so that's the irony and the magic and the wonder of AI, even if it does make us ask some hard questions of ourselves and think carefully about its impact on humanity, it actually is superior at the things we describe as personal and human, relative to humans themselves. And so that's where I'm at today. Yeah, maybe it's a bunch of fancy post rationalization, but honestly that's really where I stand.
turns.zh: 是的，我知道这是一个有趣又带点讽刺的转折。我们早期公司的使命是让互联网商务更具人性化。当我回归后，我们开始大力投入人工智能领域时，我不禁自问：这个使命现在还有意义吗？如今，我们对人工智能的投入既是出于商业需要，也是因为我们深知这是未来的趋势，人无法对抗未来——你必须融入其中。所以好吧，该死的，我们就去拥抱它。说到底，人很容易给自己编织各种小故事。所以，如果有人说这都是胡说八道，我倒愿意洗耳恭听。但当我审视自己的灵魂和思想时，我不这么认为。当我审视自己的内心和理智时，我也不这么认为。（00:13:43）但我现在坚信，为每位客户提供全天候、随时响应的专家服务——专业、快捷、亲切、风趣、友好、个性化——远比让他们等待2、3、4天才能得到敷衍的回复要人性得多。这就是人工智能的讽刺之处、神奇之处和奇迹所在。即便它确实让我们不得不严峻地审视自身，认真思考其对人类的影响，但在我们定义为"人性化"和"人性化"的领域上，它确实比人类本身更胜一筹。这就是我如今的立场。是啊，也许这只是一堆事后美化说辞，但说实话，这就是我的真实想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think data has shown people often prefer not to talk to humans just to solve problems that can just be solved. It's a lot of stress to try to figure out how to talk to some support agent that doesn't know anything about what's going on.
turns.zh: 我认为数据表明，人们往往宁愿不与真人交谈来解决那些本可以轻松解决的问题。试图搞清楚如何与对情况一无所知的客服人员沟通实在太让人头疼了。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yes, and the AI is just better. Look at Waymo. So, Waymo doesn't crash. It has 3.5 times less crashes than humans. It doesn't bother you or bug you. I like to chat with an Uber driver as much as the next guy, but not always. It doesn't have hygiene problems. It doesn't take wrong turns. I mean it just doesn't do all these things that really bug people. And it's really interesting to see Uber now offer women the option to call only female drivers, and I guarantee the reason they're doing that is because women love Waymo because they feel safer. AI is so often superior and humans are going to be far better at other things. I'm pro-human, I love humans. I really want humans in the mix for all things in the rest of my life, but when it comes to practical, productive, efficient, and effective value, the glue in between the human parts of our lives, I actually want AI and robotics.
turns.zh: 没错，人工智能就是更出色。看看Waymo就知道了。Waymo从不发生事故，事故率比人类低3.5倍。它不会让你感到烦躁或困扰。我和其他人一样喜欢和Uber司机聊天，但并非时刻如此。它没有卫生问题，不会走错路。我是说它不会做那些真正让人不爽的事。现在Uber还为女性提供仅呼叫女司机的选项，我敢打赌他们这么做是因为女性喜欢Waymo，因为她们感到更安全。这真的很有趣，人工智能在很多方面都更胜一筹，而人类将会在其他领域大放异彩。我支持人类，我热爱人类。我真心希望人类能参与我余生中的一切事务，但当涉及到实用、高效、有效的价值，连接人类生活的纽带时，我其实希望有AI和机器人技术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we start talking about how you actually made this transformation a success, one other piece of history is just your pricing strategy historically has been not liked by people. For example, I once had a Twitter poll or a survey on my newsletter just like what products do you pay the most for of all your SaaS products? And Intercom's by far the most. I know people constantly complain about just how unclear it was and how high it was, and now you guys are at the forefront of how to price AI products. So, we're going to get to that, but just talk about the lessons and what happened there with pricing back in the day.
turns.zh: 在我们开始讨论如何成功实现这次转型之前，还有一段历史值得一提——你们过去的定价策略一直不受用户欢迎。比如，我曾在Twitter上发起过调查，或者在我的新闻通讯中问过：在你们所有的SaaS产品中，哪款产品收费最高？Intercom无疑是收费最高的。我知道人们一直抱怨定价不够清晰、价格过高，而现在你们却走在了AI产品定价的前沿。接下来我们会深入探讨这个话题，但先聊聊过去定价方面的经验教训和所发生的事情。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah, so I want to just validate your survey data. Yes, people abhorred our pricing. It was a meme. There were actual funny popular viral memes on Twitter that were making fun of our pricing. Part of the problem, if not all of the problem, well, there's two problems. One was our strategy, super unfocused. As you said, we're trying to do all the things for all the people, and when you're trying to do all the things for all the people, your efforts to capture all that different types of value are going to necessitate pretty complex pricing. If you're like customer service and you're selling seats and you're doing outbound messaging and you need to charge for messages and you're doing like SD or Messenger on a website and you need to charge for leads, already that's just metrics in every direction. (00:17:49): And then if you're trying to sell to many different sizes of customers, you need tiers and gates and it just became a behemoth. So, part of the problem was the unfocused strategy, and then the other part of the problem was an unwillingness to frankly make bold decisions, say no, pick a lane and actually take pain in the short term for the long term. We rolled out this new pricing, and this is even before the Fin pricing you're talking about. When I came back and I said, "Yes, we're going to lose a lot of revenue here." I can't remember how much we wrote down, but we actually have already given away something like $50 million in ARR. (00:18:32): We've reduced the prices for a lot of customers just to give them way simpler pricing because surprise, surprise, when people feel like they have far simpler, more predictable, fairer pricing, they'll stick around longer and it creates so much more ease in the company and promotes a healthier relationship with the customer too. When our people saw that we were screwing customers effectively in every direction, it starts to erode the idea that we care about our customers and then they make other customer-unfriendly decisions. And so one of the values I promoted when I came back was that we would be customer-obsessed, and so we had to kill our old pricing and give away a lot of revenue. So, that was the spirit behind the changes. But we can talk about the Fin pricing if you want to also.
turns.zh: 是的，我只是想验证一下你们的调查数据。没错，人们对我们的定价方案很不满。这简直成了个梗。推特上有很多搞笑又流行的病毒式梗图都在调侃我们的定价策略。问题部分在于我们的策略太不聚焦了。正如你所说，我们试图面面俱到，但当你想为所有客户提供所有服务时，捕捉不同价值的努力必然会导致定价结构极其复杂。比如客服部门、座席销售、外呼营销、网站上的即时通讯服务等，这些都需要收费。（00:17:49）再比如，要想面向不同规模的客户，就必须设置层级和门槛，结果整个系统变得过于庞杂。所以，部分问题在于策略不聚焦，另一部分则在于不愿果断决策——不肯说不，选定一条路线，即便短期内会承受痛苦也要为长期发展铺路。我们推出了新定价方案，这甚至比你提到的Fin定价还要早。当我回公司后说"是的，我们会因此损失大量收入"时，我记不清具体金额了，但我们已经让出约5000万美元的年化经常性收入了。（00:18:32）我们为许多客户降低了价格，只为给他们更简单的定价模式，因为令人惊喜的是，当人们感受到更简单、更可预测、更公平的定价时，他们会留存更久，这也极大地提升了公司的运营效率，促进了与客户更健康的关系。当员工发现我们在各个方面坑害客户时，他们对我们关怀客户的信心就会逐渐瓦解，进而做出其他不利于客户的决策。所以我回归后提倡的价值观之一就是要以客户为中心，因此我们必须彻底革新旧定价体系，舍弃大量收入。这就是变革背后的精神。但如果你想听的话，我们也可以聊聊Fin定价策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's save that because that's a really important topic that I think people need to hear. Let's talk about the shift and how you made this actually happen. You make it sound like, oh, not fully, but it's oh, we have to do, it wasn't working anyway. There's no risk to go all in on this AI thing. You're making $150 million a year ARR, you're worth at least a billion dollars at that point as a business. Yeah.
turns.zh: 先暂停一下，因为这确实是个重要话题，我觉得大家需要听听。咱们来聊聊转变过程，以及你们是如何真正实现的。你说得好像不完全成功，但至少是不得不尝试，反正之前的策略也不行了。用AI彻底转型没什么风险。你们每年创造1.5亿美元的ARR，公司估值至少10亿美元。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I mean multiple billions.
turns.zh: 是的，好几个亿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Multiple billions.
turns.zh: 好几个亿。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: We were making more money than that, so we were like multiple hundreds of millions.
turns.zh: 我们当时赚得更多，所以是好几亿。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, okay. Very difficult to actually do even if things don't feel like they're growing anymore. So, first of all, just what was the moment, if there was one, of just like, okay, the six-week experiment of someone building a Fin internally, was that being like, this is it, or was there another moment of like, let's go all in on this?
turns.zh: 对，对。即使业务不再增长，彻底转型也很难。所以首先，回顾一下那个为期六周的实验，内部开发Fin产品，当时有没有一个决定性的时刻，比如"就是这样了"，还是有其他犹豫不决的时刻？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: It was the combination of the company being older, us all, me and the founders being impatient like, are we going to make something out of this? We went through a time when the company was worth a lot. We're private so we don't have a daily mark to market, but all the other public software companies dropped 80%, 85, 90%. We saw our revenue growth crater. We were used to nice double digits. We were in low single digits. And so part of it was, let's do something here. Another part of it was my own anger and dissatisfaction with how the company was being run and the mistakes that I made myself. I made a lot of compromises as a lot of founders and founding CEOs do to placate employees or do it out fear to bring investors along, following advice in the industry and best practices. (00:21:12): You betray your intuition in little bits and pieces over the years when the bright spark of your original idea turns into this big, unstoppable, scary corporate beast and a little bit of you dies every single time you go and betray yourself in that way. If you could pick in your mind three or four tech darlings from 10 years ago when you meet the CEO and talk to them privately, very few of them feel outstanding about the state of their culture and the decisions that they make and the way in which they have to work. All of them have betrayed themselves in little ways, and I had left the business, I was super sick, I was burned out frankly from the revenue even having started to slow down before I left. (00:22:05): I had been attacked unfairly in the press, just all of me was just fed up and I decided to take a very authoritarian, top-down, aggressive founder-first approach to all the things, and I found that deeply cathartic and that was the thing that led to me in part. The other was just good old-fashioned logic and the other was desperation saying, we're doing the AI thing, the AI thing, exciting and sexy. We need some new energy thing here. The new AI thing makes sense. And also just my intuition says, go for it. And so when people tell these stories, they rewrite history in their minds for the stories to be elegant and also so that they support their own self-aggrandized narratives about their brilliance. Actually, it's a big messy cocktail of things. And anyway, that's my attempt at explaining the cocktail.
turns.zh: 原因在于公司历史悠久，而我们所有人——包括我和创始团队——都急不可耐地想问：我们能否从中创造出价值？公司曾一度市值高企。虽然我们是私营公司，没有每日股价波动的压力，但其他上市软件公司股价暴跌80%、85%、90%之际，我们的营收增长却急转直下。我们原本习惯每年双位数增长，如今却跌至个位数。于是我们决定：必须有所行动。另一部分原因在于，我对公司运营方式的不满，以及自身犯下的错误。像许多创始人与首席执行官一样，我为了安抚员工、争取投资者支持，或遵循行业最佳实践，作出了诸多妥协。（00:21:12）：多年来，你会一点点背叛自己的直觉。当最初的灵感化作无法阻挡的企业巨兽，每次背叛自己时，心中的火花都会熄灭。回想十年前那些科技界宠儿，当你与他们的CEO私下交谈时，很少有人对企业文化、决策或工作方式感到满意。他们都曾在不知不觉中背叛了初心。当时我已离开公司，身心俱疲，营收放缓前就已心力交瘁。（00:22:05）：我在媒体上遭到不公指责，心力交瘁，最终采取了高压、自上而下、强势主导的管理方式，发现这释放了巨大的情绪宣泄。这也是我重振旗鼓的部分原因。另一部分原因是冷静的逻辑，还有绝望感：我们要搞AI，AI啊，多么激动人心、充满诱惑的新领域。我们需要注入新活力。直觉告诉我：放手去做。当人们讲述这些故事时，他们会美化历史，编织自我的光辉传奇。实际上，真相是一团乱麻。总之，我尽力去解析这团乱麻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a stat that when you first launched, when you first had this kind of prototype, you were losing money on every transaction that you're charging like a dollar, it cost you $120, something like that.
turns.zh: 我看到数据显示，你们最初推出原型产品时，每笔收费1美元的交易都要亏损120多美元之类的。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: That's right. 120 cents. Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。120美分。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 120 cents. Okay. So, there's a lot of vision here if this is going to get to a place where this actually will be great and affordable.
turns.zh: 120美分。好的。所以这里有很大的愿景，如果能发展到真正实用且价格亲民的阶段，那就太棒了。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: It's really funny. We charge 99 cents to resolve tickets, customer problems, and we have a higher resolution rate than anyone else, and we are proud of that and we obsess over that. It is the metric by which these agents are assessed, and we wanted our revenue to be 100% aligned with the value that they attained because we had all this scar tissue from pricing prior that felt unfair to customers. So, we said, what's the most fair that we can possibly find? Now, when we did all our research, we found that many SaaS businesses were spending between 20 and $30 per ticket resolved. We were spending 22. Now, consumer businesses, maybe they go down to $5. We were thinking, can we charge $10? That seems fair. It's half price. Can we charge $5? Can we even charge two and a half dollars? But early on we started to sense that people just wouldn't value the digital work as much as the human work, even though the digital work is better, more consistent, always available, makes the customer far happier. (00:24:49): And so we actually started to lean into a price that we thought would be was the nexus between us earning the most and it being the most palatable. We basically said that if someone is not prepared to pay 99 cent for us to rapidly and elegantly perfectly and excellently solve their customer's problem, we need to wrap this up. We don't have a business here. So, that was where the 99 cent came from. I always believe that that pricing should come from value and not from costs. The cost is our problem. We just had this sense and intuition early on that this thing will get cheaper and it got a lot cheaper. The margin moves around, but we make a margin that makes this more than worth our while, and we know our customers get an excellent deal and are able to deliver to their customers a level of service that they never could before.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。我们收取99美分来解决客户问题，但我们的解决率却比其他公司高得多，我们为此感到自豪，也非常执着于这件事。这是评估客服人员的核心指标。我们希望收入能与他们创造的价值完全匹配，因为之前的定价模式对客户来说太不公平了。所以我们思考，怎样才能做到最公平？经过调研，我们发现许多SaaS公司每解决一张工单收费20到30美元，而我们当时的收费是22美元。消费类公司可能降到5美元。我们曾考虑收10美元，但这似乎太高了，只能减半到5美元，甚至2.5美元。但很快我们意识到，人们更看重人工服务而非数字化服务，尽管数字化服务更高效、更稳定、随时可用，也能让客户更满意。（00:24:49）所以我们最终确定了一个价格点，既能让公司赚得最多，又能让客户接受。我们决定，如果有人不愿为99美分支付，让我们快速、完美、出色地解决客户问题，那我们就必须结束这项业务。所以99美分的定价由此而来。我们始终认为定价应该基于价值而非成本。成本是我们的难题。我们很早就意识到，价格会越来越低，而我们的利润空间足以让这项业务值得经营。我们深知客户得到了超值服务，也能为自己的客户提供前所未有的服务水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a very clear pitch. We just had Madhavan the podcast and the pricing expert, and he has this phrase, beautifully simple pricing is where you want to get to. Also, he's a huge fan of outcome-based pricing, which is what you're describing here, where you pay for an outcome. So, you guys are in the magic quadrant of his pricing advice.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常清晰的推销方案。我们刚刚采访了播客嘉宾、定价专家马德哈万，他曾提到"简单明了的定价才是理想的选择"。他还大力推崇基于结果的定价模式，而这正是你们所描述的——按结果收费。可以说，你们完全符合他定价建议中的"魔力象限"标准。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yes, thank God our pricing wars are over.
turns.zh: 是的，谢天谢地，我们的定价战终于结束了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Finally.
turns.zh: 终于结束了。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so going back to how you actually did this thing. So, basically you described what many people think of now as founder mode, just top down, as you said, the third area, and just here's what we're doing. We're not going to sit around waiting for you to give me ideas. What did you do? What did that look like internally?
turns.zh: 好的，回到你们实际操作的过程。基本上，你们践行了许多人眼中的"创始人模式"，也就是自上而下地决策，正如你所说的，第三个领域。你们就是这么做的。我们不会坐等你们来给我们出主意。你具体是怎么做的？内部流程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: There was a couple of things. One was we were burning a lot of money, so I cut a lot of costs aggressively. Canned a bunch of different projects. We had this big glorious office we were about to fit out and I'm like, we're about to hit negative growth territory, stop it. And a lot of companies were really stuck in the prior world where they just were used to being super successful, rich and wealthy and spent like drunken sailors. So, I stopped all of that, got really frugal in ways I never thought I would. I still haven't touched the interior design of this office. I'm in here, even though I call it the hotel Marriott, I'm sick of it. Anyway, that was one. Another was picked a lane. Strategically we were all over the place and I said, "We're doing service." Zendesk had been acquired a couple years prior. (00:27:20): They were strategically, energetically, culturally dead. They were upsetting customers in the market. There's an opportunity there. We're doing service, forget all the other stuff, even though there was a lot of people in the company saying, well, shit, we still have $80 million of ARR that we're getting from the other thing and we're really good at that, and there's a big opportunity. There's other companies in this space worth billions. It was the type of decision that where I had to practice the professional CEO approach, which is, "Hey folks, what do you all think? Let's take everyone's input. Let's put it all down on a spreadsheet." Everyone had color beside all of the different options that we may take. Let's make a group decision. I said, "Sorry, this is what we're doing." So, I was very dictatorial in that respect. We had no one making decisions, so somebody needed to, even if I had some qualms about the decisions myself, I couldn't predict the future, but someone had to make a call. (00:28:16): Obviously as soon as AI came around, I jumped hard on AI and announced that we were going to spend nearly $100 million of our own cash on that. We allocated a lot of capital, but I also restarted the culture. We had just a very comfortable culture as a lot of companies did. There was a lot of focus on social issues and a lot of complaining and dissatisfaction, and I rewrote the values designed to be a sharp knife to cut out the parts of the company that I just knew wouldn't be effective. So, I said that people must be resilient, that we had very high standards, that we'd work incredibly hard, that shareholder value was the most important thing that we'd optimize for. A lot of things that were controversial for this prior crowd. And then I designed these quarterly performance processes where not only would you get a mark or a grade for your performance against your goals that quarter, but you'd also get a score for your behavior against the values. (00:29:10): And I hard coded a formula myself, and so I took it out of the manager's hands to say, if people got below a certain mark, respectfully and lovingly, we would say, thank you for your service. We're going to go forward without you. And so you do that just a small number of quarters and you can start to shape an organization that's design and the image of the values you want to create. And obviously there was a lot of pain, a lot of satisfaction. There was attempts at soft coup, there was letters sent to the board, people really unhappy, but on the other side of it, the people left were the most incredible entrepreneurial, brave, inspiring, happy individuals you could possibly imagine. And then you hire in their image. We ran an anonymous employee survey, I think 15 or 16 months after I started aggressively working through the org and rebuilding the org and rebuilding the culture, and we had a 98 to 99% approval of management, leadership and new strategy. (00:30:19): And this is coming from me having the lowest Glassdoor rating for a CEO I had ever seen when I came back. So, I just want to explain that being that deliberate about your culture and upsetting a lot of people is the path through which you can create a culture where people are super happy, super engaged, super aligned, and now we have just this highly performant organization. Yes, we're messy in many ways. So, that was a big part of it too. So, it was kind of strategically picking a lane. Remaking how we go to market, the pricing was a really, really big piece that had a big effect. Betting on AI and then culture. And I kind of buried the AI thing because frankly none of this would matter if we didn't bet on AI. So, the story could all be summed up by saying, when you ask what did I do, it was that we built Fin and that changed everything.
turns.zh:
当时有几个关键点：首先，我们烧钱太快了，所以我大刀阔斧地削减了开支，砍掉了许多项目。我们原本有一个豪华的办公室即将装修完毕，但我对自己说："我们即将陷入负增长的境地，必须停止这种局面。"许多公司仍深陷过去的惯性思维中，他们习惯了辉煌成功、财大气粗、挥霍无度。我彻底改变了这种作风，变得前所未有的节俭。直到现在，我都没动过办公室的装修。尽管我把这里称为"万豪酒店"，但我已经厌倦了它。  

另一个关键决策是选定战略方向。我们之前战略方向混乱，目标不明确。我决定专注于服务领域。几年前，Zendesk被收购后，他们在战略、执行力和文化层面都陷入了停滞。他们在市场上激怒了客户，这正是我们的机会窗口。我们专注于服务，抛开其他杂念。尽管公司里很多人抱怨："天啊，我们还有8000万美元的ARR来自其他业务，而且我们在这方面很擅长，还有巨大的市场机会。其他同行估值数十亿美元。"但作为CEO，我必须践行专业精神："大家畅所欲言，收集所有意见，写成表格。"每个选项旁边都标注了利弊，最终由我拍板。  

（00:27:20）显然，AI兴起后，我果断投入数亿美元自有资金押注AI。我们大规模投入资金的同时，也重塑了企业文化。和许多公司一样，我们原有的文化氛围过于安逸，充斥着社会议题讨论、抱怨与不满。我重写了价值观宣言，旨在用利刃剔除那些注定无效的部门。我强调团队必须具备韧性，设定高标准，要求全力以赴，将股东价值最大化。这些举措在当时引发了巨大争议。  

（00:29:10）我亲自编写了季度绩效评估公式，规定员工不仅要对照目标完成度打分，还要根据价值观表现进行评级。我设定了硬性规则：若评分低于标准，必须礼貌但坚定地告知他们"感谢你的贡献，但我们将继续前行"。经过几个季度后，组织架构逐渐符合理想愿景。当然，过程中充满阵痛与收获，有人试图发动"温和政变"，向董事会递交抗议信，许多人离职，但留下来的人都是最具创业精神、勇气、创造力和快乐感的员工。我们还以他们的形象招募新人。我组织匿名员工调查，发现参与率高达15%或更高。
在我积极推进组织变革、重建组织架构和文化的16个月后，我们获得了98%至99%的管理层、领导层和新战略支持率。（00:30:19）要知道，我回归时曾是Glassdoor上评分最低的CEO。所以我想说明一点：刻意打造企业文化、打破旧有思维模式，才是能营造出员工高度满意、积极投入、目标一致的文化土壤的必经之路。我们如今才拥有这支高效运作的团队。诚然，我们在很多方面仍存在不完善之处，但这也是战略选择的结果。重塑市场策略、调整定价策略确实产生了巨大影响。还有对人工智能的投入——说实话，如果我们不押注AI技术，所有努力都将白费。所以归根结底，当被问及我的成就有何时，答案就是我们打造了Fin平台，而这彻底改变了一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that this was very unpopular. I imagine many people were not happy with all the change and how top-down this was, you said there was a soft coup. Is there more you could share about that? I never heard that story.
turns.zh: 你说这件事非常不受欢迎。我想很多员工对所有这些变革以及这种自上而下的决策方式都不满，你提到过一次“软性政变”。你能否详细谈谈这件事？我从未听说过这个说法。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: When you make that degree of change and you tell people that they're in control like we did in the previous generation of late-stage businesses, there's going to be some friction when you change the rules. And it's my strong belief that great employees and great companies want and are constructed out of a very clear and strong hierarchy where it is the responsibility of the CEO to make brave and hard decisions unilaterally, yes, using their experts as inputs and be responsible for the outcome. If I make decisions that propel the company in the way that thankfully my decisions have, I get rewards and kudos and I get to go back to the board and say, I want a bigger grant. If I don't, I get fired and I should get fired. If my big, brave, unilateral decisions put us in the toilet, then I have to take responsibility for that also. (00:32:30): So, that's how in my humble opinion, it should work. And I, for one, don't know of a great company that doesn't work that way. You'll see from time to time, I did this a couple of years ago, people will construct these indexes of the performance of companies that are founder led, and of course this is a self-serving statement, but it's also true. And surprise, surprise, the founder led companies perform substantially better because they have the moral authority and the willingness to take the risks that the professional CEOs don't have the remit for. The professional CEOs are typically told, don't mess things up, and the founders are bored if they're not taking the risk of messing things up from time to time. And so that's in my opinion, what creates greatness and great innovation. But like I said, there will be friction changing a company that's configured for democracy and committee decisions and soft and gentle interactions and communication to be properly founder led and top down.
turns.zh: 当你进行如此大规模的变革，并像我们上一代后期阶段的企业那样告诉人们他们可以掌控局面时，当你改变规则时难免会产生摩擦。我坚信，优秀的员工和伟大的公司都需要并建立在一个清晰、强有力的层级结构之上，首席执行官有责任单独做出勇敢而艰难的决策——当然，要参考专家的意见，并为结果负责。如果我的决策推动了公司的发展（幸好我的决策确实如此），我就能获得奖励和赞誉，然后向董事会申请更高的授权。如果做不到这些，我就应该被解雇。如果我那些大胆、果断的单边决策把公司带入困境，我也必须为此负责。（00:32:30）所以，在我看来，这才是正确的运作方式。就我所知，没有一家伟大的公司不遵循这种模式。你会时不时地看到，几年前我做过这样的研究——人们会编制由创始人领导的公司的绩效指数。当然，这可能带有自我服务的偏见，但数据确实如此。令人惊讶的是，创始人领导的公司表现明显更优，因为他们拥有道德权威，愿意承担职业CEO无权承担的风险。职业CEO通常被告知“别把事情搞砸”，而创始人如果不时冒险把事情搞砸，就会感到无聊。所以在我看来，这才造就了伟大和创新。但正如我所说，将一家习惯民主决策、委员会协商、以温和互动和沟通为主的公司转变为适当的创始人领导和自上而下模式，必然会产生摩擦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, a big lesson here is if you're trying to make the shift and it's just not moving, there's a lot of resistance. You may need to go hardcore founder mode and make some significant change. What percentage of the employees kind of turned over during this period?
turns.zh: 所以，一个重要教训是，如果你试图进行变革却进展缓慢，可能面临巨大阻力。你可能需要进入创始人模式，进行重大变革。在此期间，有多大比例的员工离职了？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Could be something ultimately like 40%. So, it was a big, big turnover over some couple number of years. Often the culture is set by a very small number of people, so it only took a quarter to really start to change the tenor of the conversations that were happening, but to bring in the people that were that new level of ambition and wanted to work as hard as the rest of us and work in a mature and engaged in excited way, that took a little longer time. There's such a thing as product market fit. There's a thing as founder market fit, there's a thing as founder, product market fit. That's how you're doing it right, but there's also such a thing as employee, founder, product market fit. You have to have the right employees for the type of business you're creating, and there are companies that want the need to be more stable and they're going to want the need to hire more stable individuals. (00:34:48): There's going to be companies that want to do the highly collaborative, more democratic thing. I wouldn't invest in them, but there's companies that want to do it. If you're an employee that enjoys that, there are a lot of positions out there. There are big companies like Google that do that. There are startups that hire the crazy, young, wild, messy, early startup people, and that's great for them and the company too. So, it's really all about having the right individuals and when you create that, not only do you create great success, but you just create a lot more happiness and balance and harmony. Ultimately, the employees who wanted a more gentle democratic environment, they're not going to be happy in a company like Intercom or Coinbase or any of these strong organizations. They'll be more happy somewhere else. So, even if it requires a little bit of a loving push out the door, I know that you're actually doing them a favor in the medium to long run.
turns.zh:
最终可能只有40%左右。所以，在过去几年里，人员流动率非常高。通常，企业文化是由少数人塑造的，因此只需一个季度就能真正改变对话的基调。但要引入那些拥有新层级雄心、愿意像我们其他人一样努力工作、以成熟且积极的方式投入的人，却需要更长时间。  

有一种叫做“产品市场契合度”的概念，还有“创始人与市场契合度”，以及“创始人、产品与市场契合度”。这才是正确的做法，但还有一种叫做“员工、创始人、产品与市场契合度”。你必须为所创办的企业类型配备合适的员工，有些公司希望更稳定，因此需要招聘更稳重的人才。  

（00:34:48）：有些公司追求高度协作、更民主的管理模式。我不会投资这类公司，但确实有企业想这么做。如果你是喜欢这种模式的员工，市场上有很多这样的职位。像谷歌这样的大公司就是如此。还有初创公司招聘那些疯狂、年轻、狂野、混乱的早期创业者，这对他们和公司都很有好处。所以，关键在于拥有合适的人才。当你营造出这样的环境时，不仅能创造巨大成功，还能带来更多幸福感、平衡感和和谐。  

最终，那些渴望更温和民主环境的员工，在Intercom、Coinbase或其他这些强大组织中是不会开心的。他们在其他地方会更快乐。所以，即便需要用温和的方式把他们请走，我知道从中长期来看，这对他们其实是一种帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to say that a lot of these people will be happier working in a different company.
turns.zh: 我本来想说，这些人中的许多人在其他公司工作会更快乐。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Absolutely. Who wants to go to war every day with your organization and in Slack? That's just not fun. That's not good for the nervous system or the soul.
turns.zh: 绝对是这样。谁会想每天在Slack上和自己的公司内斗啊？那可一点都不好玩。这对神经系统和心理健康都没好处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, so this whole period sounds very stressful for you. Did you ever regret coming back and just like, what the hell did I get myself into? What am I doing to myself?
turns.zh: 是啊，这整个时期听起来对你来说压力巨大。你有没有后悔过回来，然后想，‘我到底招惹了什么麻烦？’‘我这是在折磨自己吗？’

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I never regretted coming back, but I have many moments where I don't enjoy the job. I didn't regret coming back because it was deeply cathartic for me. When a founder runs away from their business, it is the ultimate betrayal of their heart and the dream that they have. Now, it's okay to wrap things up and quit, but when you kind of run away, like I kind of had to because I was sick and burned out and kind of disenchanted, I don't know, it didn't feel good. So, especially when I had done that, having betrayed in a million or a thousand small ways, my intuition, there was something I needed to exercise. So, it has been deeply meaningful in that respect. And then of course, I'm fortunate that it worked out. I get to be on the second most popular podcast in tech. I get to pat myself on the back in front of all these people. Who wouldn't want that? (00:37:13): That said, the reality is that for particularly people like me who like the adventure and the high agency being unilateral, day-to-day movement where you're trying to make big, wild, bold decisions, the reality is that if you're successful, most of your days will not be that. It'll be reviewing the bonus policy for next year and reviewing the comp proposal for your execs for the next year. It will be showing up for accountability meetings and stepping through the status of different work streams. It'll be rushing from meeting to meeting, having 8, 9, 10 meetings a day. I don't happen to believe that that's a great way to live your life. It'll be trying to get to all the emails you need to get to such that all those people aren't offended and hurt and trying to communicate in the ways with your staff and your team that is empathetic and thoughtful and keeps in mind that they may be having as shit a day as you are. (00:38:33): You're giving me an opportunity to paint story of this maverick led adventure that you might imagine in a comic. I'm for some reason picturing TinTin sail the seas, this swashbuckling adventure. It's not. It's corporate life kind of sucks particularly for people like me. So, I have many of those days, and so the only reason I'm still around is that I have a broader mission that makes it worthwhile for now, but that's why you see so many of our best founders get to a point where they're like, okay, I've had enough corporate fun. So, that's the most authentic answer I could give you. No regrets coming back, but plenty of pain on a day-to-day basis.
turns.zh: 我从未后悔过回归，但确实有很多时候我并不享受这份工作。之所以不后悔，是因为这对我来说是一种深层的宣泄。当一位创始人逃离自己的事业时，那是对自己内心的背叛，也是对梦想的背叛。现在，选择收手离开固然无可厚非，但当你不得不逃离——比如我因为生病、精疲力竭和心灰意冷而不得不离开——那种感觉并不好。所以，尤其是在我做过那些事之后——用无数细微的方式背叛了自己的直觉——我需要锻炼自己。在这方面，这段经历意义深远。当然，我很幸运事情有了转机。我得以登上科技界第二受欢迎的播客，在众人面前自我赞赏。谁会不乐意呢？（00:37:13）话说回来，现实是，像我这样喜欢冒险、追求高度自主、每天做出大胆决策的人，如果成功了，大多数日子都不会是这样的。他们会忙着审阅明年的奖金政策，评估高管的薪酬方案，参加问责会议，跟进各个工作进度。他们会从一个会议赶到另一个会议，一天开8、9、10个会。我不认为这是一种理想的生活方式。他们会努力回复所有邮件，避免让别人感到被冒犯和伤害。他们会以富有同理心、周到细致的方式与员工和团队沟通，时刻记住别人可能也过着和你一样糟糕的日子。（00:38:33）你让我有机会描绘出你想象中的那种叛逆冒险故事，仿佛漫画里的丁丁航海冒险。但现实并非如此。尤其是对像我这样的人来说，企业生活简直糟透了。所以，我也经常经历这样的日子。唯一让我坚持下去的原因，是我有更宏大的使命，让这一切暂时值得。但这就是为什么你会看到许多优秀的创始人最终感叹：好吧，我受够了企业生活了。所以，这就是我能给出的最真实答案。回归不后悔，但日常生活充满痛苦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today's episode is brought to you by DX, the developer intelligence platform designed by leading researchers. To thrive in the AI era organizations need to adapt quickly, but many organization leaders struggle to answer pressing questions like which tools are working, how are they being used, what's actually driving value? DX provides the data and insights that leaders need to navigate this shift. With DX, companies like Dropbox, Booking.com, Adyen and Intercom get a deep understanding of how AI is providing value to their developers and what impact AI is having on engineering productivity. To learn more, visit DX's website at getdx.com/lenny, that's getdx.com/lenny. (00:40:06): One of the interesting things about this space of agents, there's all this talk, agents are taking over. It's the future of software. SaaS is going to be replaced with agents. CX is a classic. It just feels like, I imagine looking forward, it was not obvious. Now looking back, it's like obviously this is an amazing place for agents to take over work, but there's always this talk of agents will do everything and all the SaaS software is going to be replaced by agents. Do you have a sense of just how far this disruption will go outside of CX because it's already happening in your businesses?
turns.zh:
今日节目由领先研究机构打造的开发者智能平台DX为您呈现。在人工智能时代，企业需快速适应变革，但许多管理者却难于解答关键问题：哪些工具真正有效？它们如何被应用？真正创造价值的核心是什么？DX为企业领袖提供了洞察这一变革所需的数据与见解。Dropbox、Booking.com、Adyen和Intercom等公司借助DX，深入了解人工智能如何为开发者创造价值，以及AI对工程生产力的深远影响。欲了解更多信息，请访问DX官网getdx.com/lenny（注意：网址需正确复制）。

（00:40:06）：关于智能代理领域，有个有趣的现象——人们总在讨论代理技术即将取代现有软件模式，称其是软件未来的趋势，SaaS服务将被代理所取代。客户体验（CX）领域的例子最为典型。回首往事，这一趋势看似必然，但展望未来时，人们又担心代理会包办一切，导致所有SaaS软件被彻底替代。请问您认为这种颠覆性变革除了在CX领域外，还会延伸至其他领域吗？毕竟这股变革浪潮在您的业务中已初见端倪。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: The first thing I'll say is that CX is deceptively large given it's hidden behind just two words, two letters. Customer experience really is service success, sales and marketing, in my opinion. It's all engagement with all customers. It's the biggest part by headcount of any business. Any consumer business and any B2B business the biggest organizations are sales, service, success. So, I'll talk about things other than CX in a moment, but I want to emphasize that CX is the majority of business operations. Of course, it'll go beyond CX. Any function that requires a lot repetitive operational mechanical work will be automated, whether it's chasing or collecting or issuing invoices, it could be onboarding or offboarding employees. (00:41:47): There are so many repetitive jobs in an organization that it'll start to replace. One of the interesting questions is how much will be generic operations bots, how much will be expert agents? There are expert agents for law and contract review. There will probably be expert agents for accounting, but you'll need the glue in between all of these agents too. But future organizations will be agents everywhere. I've spent quite a bit of time thinking about what does it all look like in the future, and I imagine it as a medley of humans and agents, and I don't think it's obviously going to be humans on the top and the agents all in the IC roles. I think that'll be more of a complex mix where you're going to have people that are like managers and leaders, but they'll be in IC roles, working with agents to configure them for success and monitor and manage their progress, kind of add that oversight and cover for edge cases. And so I think we're going to be surprised in which the way that these organizations go, they'll definitely be smaller, they'll be flatter because of that. (00:43:17): I won't be surprised if there are agents at the highest level too. I mean, I've been thinking about how, and we do have a great human chief of staff here, but imagine a future human chief of staff that understands your priorities and actually talks to you and does a check in each day and reaches out to different people and ask for updates and helps organize your priorities and helps you remember who you need to keep accountable. Clearly there's an opportunity for that. And so you can imagine agents in specific roles like customer service in operational roles being glue and in being kind of like co-pilot or assistant roles like that, which I mentioned. But what I think that all brings is just epic levels of efficiency. It's going to be super deflationary. There'll be a lot more competition. AI itself is insanely competitive right now. (00:44:18): It's so intense in a way that was never before that's going to come to all industries when so much of their inner workings becomes automated. And ultimately I think it's going to be great for the consumer. They'll have more options, cheaper options, and I can't but see that be great for the economy, a lot of economic lubricant as it were, and a lot of new movement and activity. And if we were to really go off the reservation, but I'll stop here, that means that we need more humans too. We need population growth to show up for this big growth economically. And yeah, I just see the future as just a beautiful collaboration between humans and agents in every direction.
turns.zh:
首先，我要说的是，CX（客户体验）看似不起眼，但其实其背后的含义远比表面理解的要深。依我之见，客户体验本质上是服务成功、销售与营销的核心，关键在于与所有客户的深度互动。就人力规模而言，它是任何企业的核心部门——无论是面向消费者的企业，还是B2B业务，销售、服务和成功部门都是最庞大的团队。当然，CX的范畴远不止于此。任何需要大量重复性操作工作的职能都将被自动化取代，无论是追款、收款、开具发票，还是员工入职与离职管理等流程。（00:41:47）组织中存在着大量重复性工作，自动化将逐步取代这些岗位。一个有趣的问题是，通用操作机器人与专家代理将各占多少比例？法律与合同审查领域已有专家代理，未来会计领域也将出现类似角色，但这些代理之间也需要有效衔接。未来的组织将全面实现代理化。我曾深入思考未来图景，设想它将是人类与代理的混合体。我认为不存在那种人类处于顶层、代理充当执行角色的简单模式。相反，这将是一个复杂的混合体——既有管理者与领导者，又会以智能协作（IC）角色与代理配合，共同制定成功策略、监督进展、处理异常情况。因此，组织形态的演变将令人惊叹——规模必将缩小、结构必将扁平化。

（00:43:17）我并不排斥最高层级采用代理的可能性。比如，我们公司就有一位出色的首席人力官，但未来可能需要更具前瞻性的角色——既能理解用户优先级、与用户深度沟通，又能每日汇报进展、协调各方、协助优先排序、监督问责机制。这种角色无疑存在巨大潜力。代理或能在特定场景中发挥桥梁作用，比如客户服务、运营岗位等，但最关键的是效率的极大提升。这将引发强烈竞争压力，人工智能领域当前的竞争已达白热化。当大量内部流程实现自动化时，这种竞争压力必将蔓延至所有行业。最终受益者将是消费者，他们将获得更多、更便宜的选择；经济也将获得巨大活力与创新动能。若要更大胆畅想（但此处不再展开），这意味着我们还需要更多的人类劳动力。要实现经济的大规模增长，人口增长势在必行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the optimism. Someone described this once as a society ... What is it? Agentic society where it's us and agents living together.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种乐观精神。曾有人把这描述为一种社会……它到底是什么？是能动型社会——就是我们和智能代理共同生活在其中。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This begs the question around just jobs. We had Marc Benioff on the podcast. He's all agent force, agent force, agent force, and asked him just like, what jobs do you think are going away? He's just like, "CX, going away, gone. Sales not going away. We need sales people." Just what's your sense? I know it's like touchy subject. No one ever wants to say jobs are going away, but just what's your sense of where jobs might be disappearing more, most?
turns.zh: 这就引出了一个关于就业的核心问题。我们在播客中邀请了马克·贝尼奥夫。他一遍又一遍地强调“代理力量、代理力量、代理力量”，并被问到他认为哪些工作会消失。他回答说：“客户体验（CX）会消失，已经消失了。销售不会消失，我们需要销售人员。” 你怎么看？我知道这是一个敏感话题，没人愿意说工作会消失，但你觉得哪些工作最可能大量消失？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I don't find it to be particularly touchy because jobs have always gone away and technology has done a really good job at stealing jobs that we're repetitive, demeaning, dangerous. We have less people losing limbs and dangerous factories or dying and suffocating down mines because of the technology that we now have available to us. People breaking their backs on farms or just doing things that's highly demeaning to the great, beautiful creative potential of each human individual life. So, I won't apologize for competing with or competing for shit work because all the while technology has done that in the past, population has increased. GDP has increased, longevity, crime rates have diminished in the western world, the world that has enjoyed the most technology. So, we have no good reason to not believe that that won't continue. Even while there is difficulty and there has been in the past, no doubt, people who were gainfully employed in dangerous work in mines had to find new work. (00:46:47): And so I don't take that for granted, but I think that this is part of the long arc of humanity flourishing and getting healthier and happier. What are the types of work that will go away? It's all the demeaning, crappy stuff, and that exists in digital businesses. You ask a human to sit at a keyboard answering the same question day in, day out, and you get to a point where you don't even ask them to answer the question manually. You ask them to click the button that brings up the macro. Like what a horrible use of a human life. I've met thousands of people that have worked at Intercom, a broad range of talents. People who they might not describe themselves as particularly high IQ. Maybe they were suited at that point in their life for this highly repetitive work. You talk to them for two or three minutes, you'll see the bright spark of a beautiful human that if they got to do the right thing, they would light up and bring so much happiness and joy to the world. (00:48:00): And so that's the mission we're all on. I'm not pollyannaish here, like I said, and I'm suggesting that there won't be friction, but for the most part, we're doing good. And to get specific, they will be CX roles and a lot of basic repetitive roles. There is a lot of repetitive stuff in sales, and so you'll do more sales with less people. There are SD or roles qualifying basic questions. You're not going to need as many people in sales organizations. So, I'm a little misaligned with Marc in that respect. But what he's getting at is that what sales people bring to the table is human connection and trust, and that is not about to go away anytime soon. And thank God for that.
turns.zh: 是啊。我倒不觉得这特别敏感，因为工作岗位一直都在消失。科技在抢夺那些重复、贬低人格、危险的工作方面做得非常出色。如今，我们不必再担心在危险工厂失去肢体、在矿井中窒息身亡，或者在农场背负重物——这些曾经高度贬低人类创造潜力的工作。因此，我不会为争夺或竞争低价值工作而道歉，因为科技过去也曾如此做过，而人口数量增加了，GDP增长了，寿命延长了，西方世界（这个科技普及度最高的地区）的犯罪率下降了。所以，我们没有理由不相信这种趋势会持续下去。即便过去存在困难，比如矿工失去工作后需要另谋生路，我们也不能因此否定技术进步的必然性。（00:46:47）所以我不把这视为理所当然，但我认为这是人类繁荣、健康和幸福长远进程的一部分。哪些工作会消失？都是那些贬低人的、糟糕的工作，而这类工作也存在于数字行业。让一个人日复一日坐在键盘前回答同样的问题，最后甚至不需要手动回答，而是点击宏命令按钮。这对人类生命来说是多么可怕的浪费。我见过数千名在Intercom工作的人，他们才华各异。有些人可能不自认为智商特别高，但他们在人生某个阶段适合做这种高度重复的工作。和他们聊两三分钟，你就能看到他们内在的美好火花——如果能让他们做正确的事，他们会为世界带来欢乐和幸福。（00:48:00）所以这就是我们共同的使命。我不是盲目乐观者，但我认为总体上我们在做正确的事。具体来说，会是客户体验相关岗位和许多基本重复岗位。销售中也有大量重复工作，所以你会用更少的人做更多销售。还有筛选基本问题的支持性岗位（SD）等角色，销售团队也不需要那么多人。所以在这点上我和马克有些分歧。但他的核心观点是，销售人员带来的客户连接和信任不会很快消失。谢天谢地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had Ben Mann, the co-founder of Anthropic on the podcast recently, and he said that he's like, "Even my job is probably going to go at some point." He was like, "Lenny, your job is going to be replaced by AI at some point." That was pretty compelling. Did not expect him to say that.
turns.zh: 不久前，我在播客上邀请了Anthropic的联合创始人本·曼恩，他说"就连我的工作也可能在某个时候被淘汰。"他还提到："伦尼，你的工作迟早会被AI取代。"这番话真让人触目惊心。真没想到他会这么说。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah, I don't know. It will in many ways. We're going to have agents in AI to aggregate content and create content, but humans, as much as when it comes to productivity, value, efficiency, efficiency is not the number one thing that we value. If efficiency was the number one thing we value, I'd always buy the cheapest clothes, furniture, computers, even paper for my printer. But I think humans value things like beauty and human stories and human heart and connection. And not only will they still want those and they'll still want a Lenny that has his own story and his own take and opinions and is a little imperfect, but they'll pay more for it. The abundance of AI is going to make automated things worth zero. Just like the value of cheap content on YouTube. Why do people subscribe to some channels and pay more? Why do people pay to rent movies? Because some things have more quality, more beauty, more craft, more art, more humanity. So, I think there'll always be a place for that.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也不确定。从很多方面来说，AI确实会取代某些工作。比如，AI智能助手可以聚合和生成内容，但人类在追求生产力、价值和效率时，效率并非最看重的东西。如果效率是首要考量，我肯定会买最便宜的衣服、家具、电脑，甚至打印机用的纸。但人类更珍视美、人类故事、人文关怀和情感联结。他们不仅会继续追寻这些价值，也会为伦尼这样有独特故事、观点和个性，虽不完美却充满人情味的人买单。AI的普及会让自动化产品变得毫无价值，就像YouTube上的廉价内容一样。为什么人们会订阅某些频道并愿意付费？为什么要花钱租电影？因为有些内容更具品质、更具美感、更具匠心、更具艺术性，更富有人情味。所以，我认为这类价值永远有其存在空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Phew. All right. I've got a couple more years at least.
turns.zh: 呼。好吧。我至少还能再干几年。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before I move on to a different topic. Just kind of reflecting back on this shift to Fin and the success that you've had, are there any other just lessons that we haven't touched on that you think might be helpful for folks that are trying to go through this journey?
turns.zh: 在转向其他话题之前，我想回顾一下你向Fin转型以及取得的成功。是否有其他尚未探讨的经验教训，对正经历这一转变的人可能有所帮助？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I think it's ultimately that you don't have a choice. My co-founder Des is writing a book at the moment, and that's core to the idea here. You don't have a choice. The story of the technology industry or digital technology is really short and it's punctuated by a small number of things, microprocessors, personal computers, the internet, maybe mobile. Now there's AI. I think AI is bigger than all these things. And all of these things disrupted essentially all categories. So, not only is this likely to disrupt all the categories, it's going to disrupt it in the most aggressive violent ways. And if you're not in it, you're about to get kicked out of all of it. And so my strongest advice is roll your sleeves up, figure out what's going to disrupt you, have fun with it. You need to bring in actual talent. We and I will be nothing if we didn't have actual AI scientists and leaders. (00:51:59): It's the only way we can be successful here. We have an incredible person who by the time this is out will have received a promotion to chief AI officer. I keep announcing all these things and that's great confidence to you. Fergal Reid, and he's just one of the very best in AI applications, and we happened to be working with him for many years. So, part of it is finding the talent and part of it is bringing in the young talent too. AI is kind of a young man's game, and I'm young, but I'm not as young as a lot of the kids building AI. And so learning to empower and enable them and learn from them too is a really big deal. And unfortunately, part of what you learn from them is the only way you're going to win right now is if you work your ass off, because all these little AI companies run by kids in their twenties are literally working 12 hours a day, literally 365 days a year. (00:53:01): No joke, all of them. And that's not a fun idea for many of us, especially those who've grown up. Some people in our generation have kids or a lot of them do. There's comfort and stability in your life. You don't want to work like that, but if you want in, that's part of the price and that's how so many of these young new AI are going to win because very few of the previous generation companies are willing to make all of those changes and go all the way in. And so my actual advice, which is not that helpful, is that if founders of previous generation companies are themselves not willing to roll up their sleeves and get into it and work as hard as the kids, hire a kid. You can be a chairperson like I was, have a lot of fun. You can mentor the kid, hire a kid because you're in the wrong job, buddy.
turns.zh: 我认为归根结底，你别无选择。我的联合创始人德斯目前正在写一本书，这正是我们今天要讨论的核心问题。你别无选择。科技行业或数字技术的发展史很短暂，关键节点屈指可数：微处理器、个人电脑、互联网，或许还有移动技术。如今AI来了。我认为AI的影响比这些技术加起来还要大。所有这些技术都彻底颠覆了几乎所有行业。AI不仅很可能颠覆所有行业，而且会以最激进、最猛烈的方式做到这一点。如果你不参与其中，注定会被淘汰出局。因此，我最强烈的建议是：卷起袖子，找出可能颠覆你的领域，享受这个过程。你需要引入真正的人才。我们团队如果没有真正的AI科学家和领军人物，就什么都不是。这是我们成功的唯一途径。我们有一位了不起的人才，等这段对话结束时，他将晋升为首席AI官。我不断提及这些成就，这对你们来说是莫大的信心保证。费格尔·里德是AI应用领域最顶尖的人才之一，我们与他合作多年。人才引进固然重要，年轻人才的培养同样关键。AI本质上是年轻人的游戏，我虽然年轻，但比不上许多开发AI的年轻人。我要学会赋能他们、向他们学习，这才是关键。遗憾的是，从他们身上学到的东西告诉我们，当下要想获胜，唯一的途径就是拼命工作，因为那些由20多岁年轻人运营的初创AI公司，每天工作12小时，全年无休。这对我们许多人来说绝非易事，尤其是那些已为人父母的人。生活需要安稳与舒适，你不愿如此拼命，但若想入局，这就是代价。这也是许多年轻AI初创公司能胜出的原因——因为老一辈公司鲜有愿意做出如此彻底变革、全力以赴的勇气。我的建议虽然不算实用，但却实话实说：如果老一辈公司的创始人自己不愿卷起袖子，像年轻人一样全力以赴，那就雇个年轻人吧。你可以像我一样当个董事长，享受乐趣。你可以指导年轻人，但归根结底，你得承认自己选错了行业，朋友。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how pragmatic this advice is and what's interesting as you talk about 12 hours a day every day, it's like we're trying to get close to what agents are doing, which is half, that's basically 50% of agents.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种务实的建议。谈到每天工作12小时，这很有意思，感觉我们正在试图接近经纪人的工作强度——毕竟他们每天工作时间就占了一半，基本相当于50%的工作量。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: But that's not just a poetic cute thing to say, that comes from something very real, which is these younger companies know how to use AI in ways that the older companies don't. The younger companies are vibe coding and using AI for their creative work and for their job descriptions. I guarantee you go to companies of our generation and even we have had to push people, you go to companies of our generation, most people in most organizations, particularly non-technical organizations, they're not using any AI. Maybe they're starting to use ChatGPT to write a job description, but they're not doing it by default. And so that's more than a joke. You're competing with young companies that are in part AI.
turns.zh: 然而，这不只是诗意的可爱说辞，而是源于一个非常现实的现象——这些年轻公司深知如何以老牌公司无法企及的方式运用人工智能。年轻公司正在将AI融入创意工作和职位描述中。我敢保证，你去我们这代人创立的公司看看，即便我们这些人也不得不督促员工。看看我们这代人的公司，大多数组织，特别是非技术类组织，他们根本没有在使用AI。或许他们开始用ChatGPT写职位描述，但这并非默认使用。这绝非玩笑话。你正与那些部分依赖AI的年轻公司竞争。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, I did an interview with the Perplexity founders. It was, I just checked, April 2024, so just over a year ago. And they were saying that the way they operated, and this sounded it's so crazy at the time, is anytime they had a question for anyone else on the team, they first asked ChatGPT about it, and then they go ask the person as like, that is insane. And now this is just obvious. That's what we all do now. Just like, hey, I'm just going to talk voice.
turns.zh: 这让我想起，我曾采访过Perplexity的创始人。仔细回想，是在2024年4月，也就是一年多前。他们提到，公司的运作方式——这在当时听起来简直疯狂——是每次团队成员有问题时，先让ChatGPT给出建议，再去找相关人员确认。这太不可思议了。而如今这已是稀松平常的事。我们现在也会这样做，比如，嘿，我要用语音助手。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: It's a prime example. They're doing many such things. When I say 365 days a year, they're the company I think of because they're doing exactly that. All these young companies are doing wild, weird and ridiculous things that people you are in my age kind of chuckle at, but it's business as usual for them. So, there's just a big mind shift, cultural shift, and there's a culture clash of the previous generation versus the new generation. And the sooner you kind of wrap your head around that, the sooner you can start to unstake yourself, I think.
turns.zh: 这就是一个典型例子。他们做了很多类似的尝试。当我提到“一年365天”时，我首先想到的公司就是Perplexity，因为他们正是如此运作的。所有这些年轻公司都在做着疯狂、奇特且荒谬的事，令我们这代人忍俊不禁，但对他们而言却习以为常。因此，关键在于尽快适应这种转变，理解文化差异，化解老一代与新一代之间的冲突。越早领悟这一点，你就能越早摆脱束缚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to build on that, the sounds crazy to work this hard, it sounds very stressful, not fun. Why would I do this? This sucks. But at the same time, this is, as you said, such an unusual rare opportunity. There's so much opportunity. There's so much wealth being created. There's so many businesses being created. This is the time, if you were to ever work really hard, this is a good time to do it.
turns.zh: 继续说下去。拼命工作听起来很疯狂，压力巨大，不好玩。为什么要这样做？这太糟了。但与此同时，正如你所说，这是一个难得的机遇。机会无限，财富正在创造，许多新企业正在诞生。如果你真想在当下努力工作，这正是好时机。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I think so. I don't actually generally promote working that hard. I try to not fetishize it. I actually think a life well-lived includes taking slow walks in nature where you're not thinking about ARR growth or hiring your chief revenue officer, not going to eight meetings a day. Maybe you should go to no meetings a day, certainly not working 12 hours a day. I don't actually promote that in general as a thing one should do with their life. I'm simply saying that if you want to compete and enjoy success in this age, which means you need to be doing AI, that is the price. (00:57:16): So, you either decide to pay the price or get out. Don't half-ass it. You see all these companies saying, we do AI and they've just sprinkle a little bit of crappy AI and they've got the same cultures. It won't work. The one thing I will say, the one little asterisk to my first point is that all great people and great things have been achieved through hard work. And so I'm speaking out of both sides of my mouth here, to younger people to let them know that every way of living is valid, but people who have achieved things have always worked hard and they find a way to enjoy it too. And particularly in 2025 in AI.
turns.zh: 我认同这一点。但我通常不鼓励拼命工作。我试图不将其神化。我认为美好的生活包括在自然中悠闲漫步，不去想ARR增长率，不操心招聘首席营收官，不参加八场会议。或许你一天不参加任何会议更好，当然更不必每天工作12小时。我并不提倡将拼命工作作为人生的常态。我只是想说，如果你想在这个时代竞争并获得成功，就意味着你必须拥抱AI，这就是代价。（00:57:16）：所以，要么下定决心付出代价，要么退出。别敷衍了事。看看那些声称自己在用AI的公司，他们只是随意加点劣质AI，却延续着原有的文化。这行不通。我想补充一点，关于我的第一个观点：所有伟大的人和伟大的成就都是通过努力工作实现的。所以我在这里也说两句话，告诉年轻人每种生活方式都有其合理性，但有成就的人总是努力工作，并且总能找到享受其中的方法。尤其是在2025年的AI时代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow this thread. I was going to ask you this earlier, but I didn't, and I want to see if this takes us somewhere interesting, just watching you speak and talk. You're very self-reflective, very centered. You have these really good breaths you take when you think about something. I met you a long time ago, randomly at a party when you were just starting Intercom. I don't think you were like that. During this kind of two-year period was there kind a transformation that you went through to kind of become this?
turns.zh: 我想参与这个话题讨论。其实我之前就想问你这个问题，但一直没机会。现在想看看通过听你说话能否获得一些有趣的启发。你很善于自我反思，也很沉稳。当你思考问题时，呼吸方式特别得当。很久以前我在一个派对上偶然认识了你，当时你刚创立Intercom不久。当时的你可不像现在这样。在这两年的时间里，你是否经历了某种蜕变，才形成了今天的模样？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Absolutely. Yeah. There's a couple things. First, I mean, there's three things that come to mind. Working in a startup for 14 years has a certain way of kicking you in the head many times a day that either kills you or makes you far stronger. So, that's one piece. There's no elegance to that point, but I think we can all intuit that that level of experience teaches you something, you grow up very fast. Point two is I did a lot of therapy. I found this amazing guy 12 years ago. He started a couple of his own tech companies and talked in public. He only coached and was a therapist to CEOs. He's now kind of in a later stage of his career. But this amazing guy, his name is Yosi Amram, amazing guy. I just landed on my feet. I just didn't know who I was dealing with. (00:59:24): But one of the greatest minds and teachers of the last, I don't know, many decades, people don't even know him, but he's taught and worked with many CEOs and he just helped me get to know me and take time for myself. And people like to hate on therapy right now. I think a lot of therapy sucks and a lot of therapists are not good. And they fear that actually therapy will lobotomize them and turn them into thumb sucking, navel-gazing, soft, irrelevant losers that won't have that edge anymore. And the interesting thing about 12 years of weekly therapy and spiritual work is that it takes your edges off, but they're all edges that are super counterproductive. All the edges that made you an asshole, got you triggered, miscommunicated or fought back when you were insecure, they take all the edges away then help you see yourself and love yourself so much more for who you are. (01:00:42): Be completely unafraid to acknowledge the things you're not good at, but own the things you are. And in understanding yourself, you understand others better and can communicate in a substantially more connected and authentic way. Great, great therapy and it has to be great, is a recipe for brilliant leadership in my opinion. And then the third part is two years away where I ran away, where I was sick, revenue growth wasn't doing so hot. I unsuccessfully tried to defend myself from a bunch of fake bullshit in the newspapers. I mean I was beat up. And in a moment like that, your ego, any sense you have of your greatness is eviscerated. And that's painful. It can be so painful that many people don't come back from it, and I credit the 10 years at that point, or nine years of therapy I did at that point, plus the support of this therapist, the coach that I had, to surviving it. (01:01:48): But if you can survive it, what you end up with on the other side is all of those insecure, a lot of the insecurities and all that ego bullshit that made you super ineffective, jealous, or triggered for all sorts of different reasons, it's gone. And your image that you are this perfect, brilliant leader that all successful founders form when they are successful had to die. And the reason that's so good is that that's so limiting. When you have this ego identity of yourself about how fucking amazing you are, then any moment that challenges that is super scary. Anyone who questions it is offensive. And so I credit wherever I am today and I have decades of learning still to go to those three components. And I feel super fortunate to have had all of them, even though the last one sucked, I can finally say, wow, it really helped.
turns.zh:
绝对的。是的。有几件事。首先，我是说，有三件事突然浮现在我脑海里。在初创公司工作14年，每天都会被各种问题反复打击，要么把你打倒，要么让你变得更加强大。第一点，这没什么高深之处，但我相信大家都能感同身受——这种经历会教会你很多东西，让你快速成长。第二点，我接受了大量心理治疗。12年前我遇到了一个了不起的人。他创办过几家科技公司，还经常公开演讲。他只为CEO们提供心理咨询和指导。如今他已步入职业生涯的晚期阶段。但这个了不起的人叫约西·阿姆拉姆，真是位奇才。我当时根本不知道自己在和谁打交道。（00:59:24）但他是过去几十年里最伟大的思想家和导师之一，尽管很多人不了解他。他教导并辅导过许多CEO，最终帮助我认识自己，学会为自己留出时间。如今人们对心理治疗颇有微词。我认为很多心理治疗效果糟糕，许多心理治疗师水平不佳。他们担心心理治疗会让人变得软弱无能，变成只会吮吸拇指、自怨自艾的失败者。12年的每周心理治疗和精神修行带来的惊喜是，它消磨了你的棱角，但这些棱角都是极具破坏性的。那些曾让你变成混蛋、引发情绪失控、误解他人或反击弱势时的棱角，都被磨掉了。随后，它帮助你接纳并深爱真实的自己。

（01:00:42）要完全不怕承认自己不擅长的事，但也要接纳自己擅长的事。了解自己，才能更好地理解他人，并以更真诚、更紧密的方式沟通。在我看来，优秀的心理治疗——必须是卓越的——是卓越领导力的秘诀。第三部分是两年前我经历的低谷：公司运营不善，病倒了，收入增长停滞。我徒劳地试图反击媒体上的虚假攻击，简直被打得落花流水。那一刻，你的自尊和对自身伟大的幻想被彻底粉碎。这太痛苦了，许多人因此一蹶不振。但归功于那时10年的心理治疗和九年的自我探索，再加上心理治疗师和教练的支持，我才挺了过来。（01:01:48）但若能挺过来，最终你会发现那些不安全感、自尊心膨胀和虚伪的自我保护机制都消失了。你曾经构建的成功创始人完美形象不得不崩塌。这种崩塌其实是种解脱，因为它太具局限性了。当你执着于自己无比牛逼的自我认同时，任何挑战这种认同的时刻都令人恐惧，任何质疑的声音都令人愤怒。所以我今天的成就，以及未来几十年仍需学习的成长，都归功于这三个关键因素。能拥有这三者，我深感幸运，即便最后一段经历糟糕透顶，但我终于能说：哇，这真的有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you for sharing all that. I'm glad I went there. I want to show you something that I randomly have in my office, my wife just got me that I think you're going to love. It's a piece of art that I think will resonate with [inaudible 01:03:02].
turns.zh: 谢谢你分享这么多内容。我很高兴我去了。我想给你看件随手放在办公室的物品，是我妻子刚送我的，我觉得你一定会喜欢。这是一件艺术品，我觉得它会引起（听不清01:03:02部分）共鸣。
