turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: May all our egos peacefully become smaller and leave this mortal coil. The reality is none of our egos ever die. And even great ... Ram Dass is this great spiritual teacher who died a few years ago and someone asked him on his deathbed something like, "How did you get over your bullshit or your ego?" And he said, "I never did. Just the edges got smoothed away." And this is a guy who had 70 years of the deepest, wildest spiritual work, he acknowledged, no, still my same self. So, the ego is still there and we actually need to acknowledge it and love it. And when you acknowledge it, then it's not a surprise when you're like a little jealous and you're like, huh, I'm jealous. That's funny. Okay. And it's all good.
turns.zh: 愿我们所有人的自我都能安详地缩小，离开这个凡尘世界。现实是，我们的自我永远不会真正死去。即使伟大的……拉姆·达斯（Ram Dass）这位几年前去世的伟大精神导师，有人临终前问他：“你是如何克服自负或自我意识的？”他回答：“我从未克服过。只是边缘部分被磨平了。” 这个人经历了70年最深刻、最狂野的精神修行，他承认，嗯，我还是同一个自己。所以，自我仍然存在，我们实际上需要承认它并爱它。当你承认它时，当你有点嫉妒或意识到“嗯，我嫉妒了”时，这并不奇怪。没关系。这一切都很美好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me Daniel Kahneman who wrote all these books about biases that we have and here's all the ways we're flawed. If people ask him, "Have you learned to live more rationally?" He's like, "Not at all." Knowing all these things about how we're flawed in the way we think all these biases doesn't actually, I can't use it in life.
turns.zh: 这让我想起丹尼尔·卡尼曼（Daniel Kahneman），他写了许多关于我们存在的偏见的书，揭示了我们思维中的种种缺陷。如果有人问他：“你学会了更理性地生活吗？”他会说：“根本没有。” 尽管了解了这些思维偏差并不能在生活中实际应用。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: We're human. We should let ourselves be human. I think it's beautiful. We're logic systems, but we're also heart systems and body systems and soul systems. So, all of it is good.
turns.zh: 我们是人。我们应该允许自己做人。我们应该接受自己的不完美。我认为这很美好。我们是逻辑系统，但我们也是情感系统、身体系统和灵魂系统。所有这些都是好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I want to go in a completely different direction. The last thing I want to talk about, I needed to mention this. I don't know if you've seen this, but I've been doing research on which companies produce the best product leaders. And I've been doing this by looking at which alumni of companies go on to become CPOs at the highest rate, get promoted the most at their next job, become the first product manager at a future startup, start their own companies. Intercom is coming number one across this research next to Palantir and Stripe, Revolut. So, the question this begs is, what are you guys doing that produces such great product leaders? There's the hiring piece and then there's what they do at Intercom piece. So, what do you think is creating these sort of really big successes from your alumni group?
turns.zh: 好吧，我想转换到一个完全不同的方向。我想谈谈最后一点，我需要提到这个。我不知道你是否看过，但我一直在研究哪些公司能培养出最优秀的产品负责人。我的研究方法是观察哪些公司的校友最有可能晋升为首席产品官（CPO），或者在下一份工作中获得最多晋升机会，成为未来初创公司的首位产品经理，或者创办自己的公司。在这项研究中，Intercom与Palantir、Stripe、Revolut并列排名第一。那么，这引发了一个问题：你们做了什么才能培养出如此出色的产品负责人们？这既包括招聘环节，也包括Intercom内部的培养机制。那么，你们认为是什么造就了这些校友群体中如此显著的成功案例呢？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah, I don't have a really succinct answer unfortunately. I can say in the abstract, our culture is a very producty culture. So, myself and Des, there was four founders and me and Des Traynor drove a lot, like all the strategy. We're product guys. I was a software designer. I studied computer science, so I'm technical, but never did it professionally. So, the first part is that just product innovation, design just was just core to our culture and people always picked up on that. So, I think good people wanted to work here and we were good at finding good people. The other part was that because we had this sprawling strategy, we had all these products that we needed a complex structure for it and that included lots of PMs and PM groups that we gave a lot of autonomy to. And so the product of our big messy strategy was that we had PMs that got to act like mini CEOs. (01:06:27): And so I think that they got to learn the broader skill sets beyond designing wireframes and interviewing some customers. They really own it like a mini CEO to some degree. I think there's one other thing which is part to our approach was this deeply first principles thinking methodology almost to a fault, although I don't think it's a fault. I and we would create frameworks for everything. It's like, okay, we want to do these events. Who are the events for? What is the ultimate goal of the event? What's the mechanism by which events work? What are other mechanisms that can achieve that same goal? How do we define success for an event like that? How does the user or the attendee define value? What other things do those people find valuable? We create these complex systems to try and approach everything, but the net effect was we'd have really joined up considered strategy and it's everywhere. (01:07:36): Like Paul Adams, our chief product officer, I didn't even plan to show this. He made this book recently, The AI Age and the Transformation of Customer Service and it's a bunch of frameworks for how to think about AI, et cetera. So, it's part of what we do. And so we would hire people who are good at that, but we teach that. That's teachable and not everyone does that. And so the conversations that Des and I would have, we still love being on whiteboards. Our very first office, our own office in Dublin, it was a tiny office. One wall was four, five computers, the other wall was just all whiteboards. We loved that we had a whiteboard wall. In our next office we had a room, square room and all walls were whiteboards. (01:08:24): So, we just love to draw diagrams so you can teach all that stuff. So, yeah, it's just all that good energy product, product energy, first principles, the people we chose. And on the founders side, I was talking to Des about this morning, why have so many Intercom people gone on to be founders? I think it's because we hired founder types and my pitch to people was always come to Intercom, figure out how great companies are built and build it with us and then go on to start your own. I would say that often at all hands. But the irony is that the people we hired back then, the founder types were probably not great employees. They were better founders. I'm not a good employee. And so it'll be interesting to see if this current cohort, we'll get many founders out of this current cohort, but will they convert as well as they did before? (01:09:16): Because we're now hiring people who want to be part of something bigger. They're more mature and grown up, more stable and consistent. They're part of, they have a certain expertise and a certain lane they want to work in. And maybe they're not the crazy types that went on to start companies, but it's wild. I did see some of that research by you, particularly the one where you show the companies ranked by the number of founders that they have. And I'm like, what is happening? I was as surprised that we were that high as you were because there are many other great companies on that list. So, surprised and proud.
turns.zh:
是的，很遗憾我没有一个简洁的答案。我可以抽象地说，我们的文化是一种非常注重产品创新的文化。所以，我和德斯（Des Traynor）等四位创始人负责了大量战略工作，我们都是产品人。当时我是一名软件设计师，学过计算机科学，所以具备技术能力，但从未从事过专业开发。因此，首先，产品创新和设计是我们文化的核心，人们总能感知到这一点。因此，优秀人才愿意加入我们，而我们也善于招揽优秀人才。另一方面，由于我们实施了庞杂的战略，开发了众多产品，因此需要为其建立复杂的组织架构，这就包括赋予许多产品经理和产品团队高度自主权。这样一来，我们庞杂的战略所带来的结果就是，产品经理们得以像小型CEO一样自主运作。（01:06:27）我认为，他们需要掌握超越设计和客户访谈等基础技能的更广泛能力，在某种程度上像小型CEO一样承担责任。我认为还有一点很重要，那就是我们的方法论深深植根于第一性原理思维，尽管我不认为这有什么问题。我们为一切事务构建框架。比如，我们想举办活动——活动面向谁？活动的最终目标是什么？活动的运作机制是什么？还有哪些机制能实现相同目标？如何定义此类活动的成功标准？用户或参与者如何定义价值？他们还认为哪些东西有价值？我们构建这些复杂的体系来全方位思考问题，最终形成了贯穿全局的统一战略。（01:07:36）比如，我们的首席产品官保罗·亚当斯（Paul Adams），我甚至没打算展示这段内容。他最近出版了《AI时代与客户服务变革》一书，书中汇集了思考AI等问题的框架体系。这正是我们文化的一部分。因此，我们会招聘擅长这方面的人才，但也会传授相关技能。这并非易事，并非所有公司都这样做。德斯和我之间的对话，我们至今仍喜欢在白板上交流。我们在都柏林的第一间办公室非常小，一面墙摆着四五台电脑，另一面墙全是白板。我们喜欢那面白板墙。在后续办公室，我们建了一个方形房间，四面墙都是白板。（01:08:24）所以，我们就是喜欢画图，这样能把所有知识传授出去。是的，这就是产品文化的活力——产品能量、第一性原理思维，以及我们选对了人。从创始人角度说，我今天和德斯聊到，Intercom为何有这么多人后来成为创始人？我认为是因为我们招聘了具有创业思维的人才，我向他们宣传的理念是来Intercom，了解优秀公司的构建之道，与我们共建，然后再去创办自己的公司。我经常在全员大会上强调这一点。但讽刺的是，当年我们招聘的那些具有创业思维的人才，可能并非优秀的员工。他们更适合当创始人。我倒想看看如今这批员工中，有多少人能成为优秀的创始人，他们的转化率是否能与过去相比？（01:09:16）因为我们现在招聘的都是想参与更宏大事业的人才。他们更成熟、稳重、稳定，也具备一定的专业能力和洞察力。
他们想进入的行业领域。或许他们不像那些疯狂创立公司的家伙，但这种现象实在令人惊叹。我确实看过你做的一些研究，尤其是那份按创始人数量对公司进行排名的报告。我当时就想，这到底是怎么回事？看到我们公司的排名如此靠前，我和你们一样感到震惊，毕竟榜单上还有许多其他优秀的公司。所以，既惊喜又自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love when people say, I don't really have a clear answer. And then you have exactly a clear answer and it resonates a lot with other companies on this list that I've had on of what the themes are, and I'll just reflect back a few of them. One is complexity. That comes up a lot. And interestingly, most of the other companies in the list, I'll read them real quick. Intercom, Palantir, Revolut, N26, Dropbox, Chime, Stripe, and then Coinbase and Notion is down there. So many are FinTech. Almost all are FinTech. And the complexity there is really high. So, there's a really interesting trend there. Just complexity. Ownership is another one that comes up a lot. Many CEOs, GMs kind of roles, first principles thinking and just going to the bare metal comes up a lot in these conversations.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢听到人们说："我真的没有一个明确的答案。"然后你却给出了一个清晰的答案。这让我对这份榜单上的其他公司产生了共鸣，我想探讨一下他们的核心主题。我先快速列举几个：首先是复杂性，这个话题频率很高。有趣的是，榜单上的其他公司——我快速浏览了一下：Intercom、Palantir、Revolut、N26、Dropbox、Chime、Stripe，还有Coinbase和Notion——很多都是金融科技公司，几乎全是金融科技公司。他们的复杂性确实很高。这里有个很有意思的趋势，就是复杂性。所有权也是一个常被提及的议题。许多CEO、总经理之类的角色，坚持第一性原理思维，直击核心问题的做法，在这些对话中频频出现。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then hiring senior people, hiring founder types.
turns.zh: 然后是招聘高级人才，招募创始人型人才。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yes. Like Stripe did a lot of that. I think Stripe did a lot of first principle stuff and founder types.
turns.zh: 是的。比如Stripe就做了很多这方面的工作。我觉得Stripe在第一性原理和创始人型人才方面下了不少功夫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thing, we didn't even talk about this, but you guys invented RICE. You guys popularize jobs to be done. Like speaking of frameworks, you guys are a wealth of frameworks that we all use.
turns.zh: 另外，我们甚至没聊到这个，但你们发明了RICE模型，还推广了"待办事项"理念。说到框架，你们简直是框架宝库，我们都用着你们的框架。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Drowning and frameworks, yeah.
turns.zh: 被淹没在框架中，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Drowning slash changing the way everyone builds product in a really positive way. Okay, is there anything else that you wanted to touch on or leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 被淹没/以一种积极的方式改变了所有人构建产品的方式。好的，在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，还有什么想和听众分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: When someone like me comes on a podcast like this, they always have an ulterior motive and that's healthy and good. It's part of the transaction. Some of it is to enjoy feeling like an expert. But my ulterior motive today is to make sure that people understand that Intercom is a fundamentally different type of late stage company. We are a large old startup. Every single way in which we work is as a startup and are competing with and crushing the actual startup competition in our agent categories. And the reason that that's important for people to know is just like I said earlier, that the handicap that good but late stage companies have is that their late stage and people don't mentally put them in the same box. (01:12:10): They just don't imagine these older companies. If I told you that IBM had made the most wildly innovative coding assistant, you'd find it hard to believe, most people would. It's maybe so interesting such that it would stick in your mind, you need to go look at it. But by default people aren't going to look at IBM. And so I want people to take a new look at Intercom because it's a brand new company and our mission is to help every single type of business deliver impeccable, incredible, beautiful personal service to every single one of their users and people, many thousands of people are using Fin for that today. So, go check out Fin please, fin.ai.
turns.zh: 像我这样的人参加这种播客，总有不可告人的目的，这很正常，也是交易的一部分。部分是为了享受专家的感觉。但我今天的真正目的是确保人们明白Intercom是一家根本不同的晚期阶段公司。我们是一家大型老牌初创公司。我们的一切工作方式都像初创公司，在我们的代理类别中与真正的初创公司竞争并碾压他们。人们需要知道这一点的原因，正如我之前所说，优秀但处于晚期阶段的公司面临的一个障碍是，他们的晚期阶段和人们的心理定位不一致。（01:12:10）：人们很难想象IBM开发出最具创新性的编码助手，大多数人都会觉得难以置信。这可能很有趣，会让你印象深刻，你需要去看看。但默认情况下，人们不会去关注IBM。所以我想让人们重新审视Intercom，因为它是一家全新的公司，我们的使命是帮助每一家企业为他们的每一位用户提供无可挑剔、令人惊叹、美好的个性化服务，如今已有数千人使用Fin实现这一目标。所以，请去看看Fin，fin.ai。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I don't know if you mentioned this at the beginning, but let's mention that you predict that you'll be the fastest growing company across if you were to look at all public software companies next year.
turns.zh: 我不知道你是否在开头提到过，但让我们提一下，你预测如果明年观察所有上市软件公司，Intercom将是增长最快的公司。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: So, two years ago we were in the low single digits growth rate. We doubled our growth rate and last year we were in the low double digits. This year we're in the 15th percentile of all public software companies. So, you take the 120 something public software companies, we're in the 15th percentile. So, we're getting up there fast and if we sustain this trajectory, and it's obviously dangerous to put these types of things out publicly, but I'll tell you, I look at the charts and it's hard not to imagine where this goes. I think we're going to find ourselves being the fastest growing out of all, relative to all public software companies. So, let's see. But that's the level of shock, surprise and transformation that has actually happened here all because of Fin. So, check in with me in a year and maybe I'll be embarrassed or maybe I'll be feeling like a genius.
turns.zh: 两年前，我们的增长率还处于个位数。去年我们将增长率提升至两位数，今年我们在所有上市软件公司中排名第15位。也就是说，如果把120多家上市软件公司放在一起，我们的排名位列第15位。我们正以惊人的速度崛起，如果能保持这种势头——当然公开谈论这些目标可能不太明智——但我必须说，看图表时不难想象未来会如何。我认为我们将成为所有上市软件公司中增长最快的公司。拭目以待吧。但这正是Fin所带来的震撼、惊喜和变革。一年后再来见证，或许我会觉得自己像个天才，或许又会感到无比自豪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or underselling it. This just reflects back on exactly how I started our conversation. You've done something extraordinary at Intercom. I'm really happy that we're here and we're sharing this story.
turns.zh: 或者说我低估了它。这正好印证了我开场时所说的观点。你在Intercom做了一件非凡的事。很高兴能与大家分享这个故事。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Please. Ready.
turns.zh: 请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常向他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: So, I found I lost the habit of reading as I started to get more and more stressed with my startup. And so I would listen to audiobooks here and there, but the most recent book I read is a book called Nuclear War: A Scenario, and it's a very much a nonfiction and scared the shit out of me. So, if you like nightmares, it'll be beautiful bedtime reading.
turns.zh: 我发现随着创业压力越来越大，我已经失去了阅读的习惯。偶尔听听有声书，但最近读的书是《核战争：一种情景》，这是一本非虚构作品，把我吓得不轻。如果你喜欢噩梦般的场景，那这本书绝对是绝佳的睡前读物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Excellent.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近你看过或喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I love movies. I want TV to be better, but I very rarely find TV to be great. The first and last TV show I loved was True Detective one that was just incredible. But the last movie I watched was 28 Years Later, and that's by Danny Boyle. I was born in the eighties, grew up as a kid in the nineties, and so grew up with Trainspotting. It was 28 Days Later. Then he made a movie called Sunshine. So, 28 Years Later is a type of movie that's just not made anymore. It's the most nineties movie made since the nineties. It's like very rock and roll and also deeply touching. So, I was really surprised by that. I bet I would love to know that younger generations that are watching this, what they may think, they may hate it, but I love 28 Years Later.
turns.zh: 我喜欢电影，但很少觉得电视剧出色。我最爱也最难忘的电视剧是《真探》，那部剧简直令人惊叹。但最近看的电影是丹尼·博伊尔的《28天后》。我出生于80年代，90年代成长，深受《猜火车》的影响。这部《28天后》堪称90年代的缩影，充满摇滚精神又饱含深情。看完后我很惊喜。我敢打赌，年轻观众看完后或许会讨厌它，但我超爱《28天后》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, this is the same person that made 28 Days Later, then 29 years later [inaudible 01:15:51].
turns.zh: 对，就是拍过《28天后》的丹尼·博伊尔，29年后[音频1:15:51]。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah, Danny Boyle.
turns.zh: 对，就是丹尼·博伊尔。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. Very cool. I didn't know about that. Do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love? Could be a gadget, could be an app, could be clothes.
turns.zh: 哇。好酷。我都不知道这回事。最近有没有发现特别喜欢的产品？可以是小玩意、应用程序或服装。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I very rarely like products, I'm such a perfectionist that it has to be really simple with very little moving parts, like a bowl, to actually be like, good. I've started to get more into coffee. I've been buying products by Fellow. They're remarkably good for consumer products, different, it's on a different level. So, there's some sort of level of taste and craft happening there that I don't see in basically any other consumer hardware type products. And of all things, I'd bought a Porsche 911 recently and that is a beautiful product. The interiors are exquisite and there's still a bunch of shit that is going to annoy you. And so it's far from perfect. So, yeah, perfectionism is sometimes a gift if you're in the business of creating products, but also quite the curse. You're never happy, including with the Porsche 911.
turns.zh: 我很少会喜欢某款产品。我是个完美主义者，产品必须设计简洁，活动部件越少越好，这样才算真正优秀。我最近开始对咖啡感兴趣，一直在购买Fellow品牌的产品。他们在消费类产品方面表现出色，独树一帜，完全超出常规水准。就产品设计而言，Fellow的产品在口味和工艺方面都堪称典范，这在其他消费类硬件产品中实属罕见。说到这里，我最近刚买了一辆保时捷911，这款车确实是个优秀的产品。内饰精美无比，但仍有一些让人不爽的小毛病，总体而言远非完美。说起来，如果你是从事产品设计的人，或许完美主义有时是种天赋，但也可能是个魔咒。完美主义者永远不满足，即便面对保时捷911这样的产品也是如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's the third time someone recommended a car. Someone recommended, I think Boz at Facebook recommended a fancy Mercedes, and then someone once suggested a Rivian, so now we got Porsche on the list. I always thought maybe one day I'll give someone all the prizes, all the products people have ever mentioned in this. And those are getting, Porsche might be a little high. Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find yourself repeating, coming back to in work or life sharing with friends?
turns.zh: 我想这是第三次有人推荐车了。有人推荐过，我记得Facebook的Boz推荐过豪华的梅赛德斯-奔驰，还有人提过Rivian，现在又轮到保时捷了。我一直觉得，或许有一天我会把所有奖品都送出去，把大家提到的所有产品都送给别人。不过保时捷可能有点太高级了。好，我还有两个问题。你有没有最喜欢的座右铭，经常在工作或生活中回想？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: It's trite. It's not sophisticated and it's more of a concept than a phrase, but it's something around the idea that life is short. I'm just so aware that time ticks by and we all live on autopilot. So much of what we do is inspired by either our insecurities or things that other people we look up to or envy do. Very rarely making contact with what we really want and following our hearts and our heads. And we just kind of get stuck in these lanes and just live out our days. And certainly when you get 41 now, you get to 41 and thankfully still very young, anyone in their forties, congrats, should feel good about that. (01:18:18): But I know if you're in your twenties or thirties, 40 feels old. But when you're in your forties, my experience is that the weeks and the months and then the years go by. It's not a big deal. I'm back at Intercom two and a half years now to any of these kids in AI in their twenties. If they don't get something done or achieved by next month, they'll be so disappointed themselves and so impatient. And in some ways, at least when it comes to productivity, they're better at getting more out of the time. But I'm now trying to get more life out of the time too. So, just, if there is a motto, it's like life is short or memento mori, we're all on the way out. So, make the use of what you've got.
turns.zh: 这听起来挺老生常谈的，既不深刻，也算不上名言，更像是个概念而非具体句子。但核心思想是生命短暂。我深知时间飞逝，而我们都像在自动驾驶状态下生活。很多行为源于不安全感，或是模仿我们敬仰或羡慕的人。但我们很少触及内心真正渴望的东西，追随自己的心意和理性。我们就这样被困在既定轨道上，日复一日地度过时光。如今41岁的我，庆幸自己还算年轻（01:18:18），但我知道如果你二十多岁或三十岁，觉得40岁很老。但到了四十岁，我的经验是，周月年时光如流水般逝去。这没什么大不了的。两年半前，我重返Intercom，看到那些二十多岁的AI工程师，如果下个月前没完成任务或取得成果，就会倍感失望和焦急。从某种程度上说，至少在生产力方面，他们更善于利用时间。但如今我也想在生活中更高效地利用时间。所以，如果说有什么座右铭，那就是生命短暂，或者“纪念死亡”，我们终将离去。所以，珍惜当下所拥有的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fun fact, I built an app once called Savorable that helped you savor the moment, it was called Savorable and it sent you a text every few hours, I don't know, maybe once a day with a little reminder of way to savor the moment. And one of the texts was just like, remember, you will die.
turns.zh: 趣事是，我曾开发过一个叫Savorable的应用，帮助人们享受当下，每隔几小时（或许一天一次）就会发送提醒短信。比如，记住，你终将死去。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah. And the problem is that even that idea, we forget it instantly. And if you start getting text every day, you'll ignore the text. Try to fault. We just don't want to acknowledge that reality on a day-to-day basis. Maybe that's important.
turns.zh: 是啊。问题是，即便有这样的理念，我们也很容易忘记。每天收到提醒短信，你也会选择忽略。我们就是不愿日复一日直面这个现实。或许这很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, maybe for the best.
turns.zh: 是啊，或许这样最好。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, Final question. Speaking of apps, I was doing research on you in preparation for this and I didn't realize you built Quitter back in the day. I love Quitter. I found it so fun. It basically told you anytime someone unfollowed you on Twitter. So, the question just what happened to that app?
turns.zh: 好的，最后一个问题。说到应用程序，我在为这次访谈做研究时发现，你曾开发过Quitter这款应用。我超爱Quitter的，觉得它特别有趣。它基本上能随时提醒你，Twitter上有人取消了对你的关注。所以我想问问，那款应用后来怎么了？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I think we eventually sold it for 14K.
turns.zh: 我记得我们最后以1.4万美元的价格把它卖掉了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's cool.
turns.zh: 哇，真不错。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: On one of these, I think there's a website called Flipper where you could sell websites. It really blew up. It was like a little experiment, kind of a social experiment. It was the first time that I had this feeling that there's no reason someone wouldn't want to use this. Obviously people are going to want to use this. And it was really instructive for me because it taught me that that feeling is possible. You meet so many founders, young founders particularly, and they don't have a sense within themselves about the value of the stuff they're building. Will this be good? Let's get customer feedback. And it is possible to build things that you deeply know makes sense. And that's why my formula for building things was to always build things for myself. And that was what Quitter was like. Followers go up, followers go down. At that point in time, people had 100 followers or 200 followers, and you'd want to know who's not my friend anymore.
turns.zh: 我记得当时有个叫Flipper的网站，可以在上面卖网站。它当时火得不行。这其实就是个小实验，社交实验。我第一次感受到，人们肯定会喜欢用这个产品。显然人们会愿意用它。这真的让我深受启发，让我明白这种感觉是可能存在的。你会遇到很多创业者，尤其是年轻创业者，他们对自己产品价值的判断不够自信。产品市场适配性好吗？先收集用户反馈吧。但其实有些东西你自己深知是有意义的。这就是为什么我创业的秘诀就是先为自己做产品。Quitter就是这样的。粉丝增加，粉丝减少。在那个时候，人们有100个粉丝或者200个粉丝，你就想知道谁不再是你的朋友了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I love that that was your bar that led you to the success later if it's as good as Quitter in terms of product market fit.
turns.zh: 天啊，我真希望你当时的那个标准能延续到后来的成功案例上，比如Quitter这样的产品市场适配性极佳的应用。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: I mean, it had the best fit ever. About everyone on Twitter tried to sign up for it and it broke.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，它的产品市场适配性堪称完美。当时Twitter上几乎所有人都想注册，但服务器崩了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I loved it. Eoghan, thank you so much for doing this. I love just how real and open you are about everything and just how much insight you have to share. I also just love the vibe. I feel like I just am more centered just watching you-
turns.zh: 不过我超爱它的。Eoghan，非常感谢你参加这次访谈。你对一切都如此坦诚，分享了如此深刻的见解，整个氛围太棒了。我觉得自己看你讲话时更能静下心来——

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Oh, thank you.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... speak. Two Final questions. Where can folks check out Fin, follow you if they want to follow up on anything? And then how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: ……最后两个问题。读者们在哪里可以了解Fin？如果想跟进相关信息，可以关注你吗？还有听众们如何能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Check out Fin, fin.ai. If they want to follow me. I'm E-O-G-H-A-N on Twitter, so it's Irish spelling of Owen. But if they want to be helpful to me, I'd love them to try Fin. I'd love them to have their friends that run any kind of customer operations, try it too. This AI thing is noisy. There's so much hype, but it's also really real. And the weird thing about Fin, even relative to the coding apps, the coding apps are blowing up, and yet there's a lot of people experimenting and kicking tires. You can't kick tires with Fin. We only deliver value when you expose it to your customers and it closes tickets and makes them happy. And so AI is really, really happening. And so if you know anyone out there that has customers, they should be using Fin. It's the smartest, cheapest, easiest way to dramatically enhance their business. So, if they do that, they'll be helping me sincerely.
turns.zh: 可以去fin.ai看看。如果想关注我，我在Twitter上的账号是E-O-G-H-A-N，爱尔兰拼写的Owen。但如果听众们能帮到我，最好试试Fin。特别是那些负责客户运营的朋友们，应该也值得一试。这款AI产品虽然很热闹，宣传很多，但它确实很实用。Fin的特别之处在于，即使相较于编程类应用（那些应用现在也很火），也有很多人在尝试和探索，但Fin不一样。只有当你把它展示给客户，解决客户问题，让他们满意时，它才能创造价值。AI真的正在落地。所以如果有认识有客户的朋友，应该用用Fin。这是提升业务最智能、最便宜、最简单的方式。所以如果他们这么做了，就是在真心帮助我了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm sold. Eoghan, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 我被说服了。Eoghan，非常感谢你今天的分享。

turns.speaker: Eoghan McCabe
turns.en: Thank you, sir. Pretty fun.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，先生。真的很有趣。
